strong ot purpose—such a face as women love. Clean shaven men do not look their best with a three days' growth of beard on them, but he looked better than most men would have done. His rugged strength did not suffer from mere untidiness. His soiled shirt, collarless, and flung open at the front showed off his muscular neck to advantage.

A BROAD stretch of the South Pacific, smooth as glass and burnished like a shield of blue steel. A sky of blazing light, fierce, pitiless, and with never a fleck of cloud to break its surface, or cast a single shadow on the waters beneath. A small black speck on the face of the deep, crawling slowly like a wounded animal that is swimming its last strokes before its strength fails. The small black speck was a boat contain- ing five men and a boy, the sole survivors of the "White Swallow." Three days ago she had been a soo ton brig bound. from Cardiff to Lima. She was now a charred mass of timber burnt to the water's edge, and out of her crew of twenty-four men six alone re- mained. It was doubtful if it would not have been better for them to have gone down in the storm which had overtaken their com- rades in the other boats. They had only provisions for a week and had had but little time to save anything from the wreck. The clothes they wore, a compass, a rifle, and fifty
Such were the survivors of the "White Swallow," bound together by common mis- fortune, and working in shifts night and day to reach land before their food was exhausted.

They steered their course sou'-west by west in the hope of striking Easter Island or one of the islands of the Marquesas Groups They were without a chart, for it had been put in one of the other boats. But judging from what Captain Williams could remember, they were at least 700 miles from land. They had barely a week's provisions, and unless they happened to fall in with a ship, things looked very bad for them. They kept their spirits up, however, and Winkles, who was of little use In moving the boat, told them anecdotes of his early days in Whit,echapel that promised well for his future career.
but these were motionless. The sight reminded them horribly of a spider and four dead bluebottles.
cartridges, the log of the ship, and a mongrel istituted their sole possessions. The us a mere incumbrance to them, but leen impossible to leave it to roast to death.

For five days there was no wino, an re skin on their arms and faces blistered like new paint. Then a breeze sprung up from the west, and drove them out of their reckon- ing in a single night.. It continued for twenty- four hours and then died away. They could only guess that they were rather west of their course, and steered due south. They eked out the food, but at the end of' another three days they had only a pound of biscuits and a quart of water for each man of them. They made this last for two days more, and then death began to look them in the face. They were making slow progress. Men do not row very well on half a pound of biscuits a day, and it is thirsty work sitting under a tropical sun. Tredegar kept his last biscuit and looked at it for eight hours. Then he gave a foolish laugh and ate it. 'Perhaps he would have kept it longer if it had not bcen for the others. He could not stand the look in their eyes as they glared at him. - After. that everyone's attention was fixed on the dog. The poor beast was half dead already, and it was a mercy to kill him. The men had given him a. good share of their food, and it was only reasonable that he should make some return to them. But they all felt like cannibals, and Winkles burst into tears. He had an idea that it would be his turn next, He had read a good many stories of shiplipecked sailors, and in these the boy was always the first to go. Then for a whole day they were without food or water, and not one of them had the I:4tli to take a hand at the oars. T:J

waiting till the morning. Even at that !distance they could hear the thunder of the waves on the iron bound coast, and see the white spray foaming on the rocks. Hughes cried out with parched lips that he would rather drown than endure his agony, and tried to . jump overboard. Tredegar held him down, and kept his grip on him through all the night. . . .
latter it had

Captain Williams, a hard, sullen old sailor, who had seen the very worst days of the merchant service, sat in the stern of the boat and made little entries in the log with the stump of an old lead pencil. By his side sat the boy. The latter was slight of frame and there was a smile on his thin wizened little face. He was anticipating adventure, and he it was who had saved the rifle and cartridges. having a sweet vision of meeting savages on a desert island. He was called . Winkles, and responded to no other name. In the bows ot the boat were two seamen, Morgan and Hughes. They were rough fellows, but they had fallen asleep, and there was something almcist soft and pathetic in their faces. Two men were pulling at the oars. One was Dennis, second mate of the ship, a lean slip of a man, but with the wiriness and the activity of a cat. The other was Emrys Tredegar, who had shipped as a passenger on the "White Swal low" to Lima. He was a young man of about thirty'. of enormous bulk and strength. He was 6 ft. 4 in. in height, and was so powerfully built that he seemed merely a stalwart fellow of no extraordinary stature. His great, arms were bare almost to the shoulders, and the mmnles showed up like knots and ropes of steel. As he drove the oars through the water they bent like whips. His face was not handsome, but kindly and honest, and
All the men were absolutely worn out, but no one closed his eyes. The nights were short, yet that one seemed an eternity.

When dawn broke it disclosed a black wall of rock nearly three hundred feet in height, rising sheer from the foaming waters at its base and crowned with thick forest. They lifted their sail again to the slight breeze and skirted the coast tzt a distance of half .a mile. The island appeared to be about [seven miles in length, and they sailed half round it before they came to a sheer break in the cliffs. It appeared to ran inland for about a mile.

'This ravine was not more than a hundre..-I yards in width, and as they sailed down it the dark water seemed like the aisle of some great c:--thedral with towering walls of stone and n. roof of sapphire blim The summit was still fringed with forest, and the air was bright with the wings of millions of butterflies and gauzy insects. The water was now almost entirely covered with the large patches of floating spiders. But although the whole place was musical with the hum of insects, it was noticeable that not a single bird crossed the vault of heaven or hovered about the cliffs, and not a single
imENENAMIIi

Before they had gone very far, Hughes grasped him by the arm and pointed into the heart of the wood. They both stopped, and saw in till: distance the strands of the giant web like fine threads against a clear piece of sky. in their centre was a large dark patch with four arms or legs. Ike the figure of a man clinging to a wall and, as they looked, it seemed as though the limbs moved. Nearer the edge of the web were four other patches

(hate pangs of starvation. Then they cooked the rest over a fire, and had three more apiece. • Then Captain Williams loaded the rifle and looked wistfully at the fringe of forest. It was as silent as the grave, and not a cry of bird or beast came from its depths. Not even a butterfly came out of its darkness into the sunlight. All insect life seemed to have died away by this silent pool.. "I will try what I can do," Captain Wil- liams muttered, rising with difficulty to his feet, "We must have some meat. One of you had better come with me. Morgan, you look as if you could walk. Maybe you can help to carry all I can shoot." With these words he struggled off towards the forest. Morgs.n followed him, carrying a piece of stick which he had found on the beach. The ;others watched the two men picking their way among the boulders until they reached the trees. Then they saw Mor- gan draw a knife from his belt and cut a notch in a huge palm. Hungry and eager though the two men were, they had not for- gotten the precaution of making their path: Then they disappeared from sight; and in the silence their companions could hear the rustling of leaves, and the snapping of twigs for several minutes afterwards. Then all sounds died away. Then they lay on their backs in the sun, and longed for something to smoke. Tred- egar had a single cigar in his pocket, but he was kind-hearted enough not to enforce his right of possession and smoke it. He

div.head: he Examiner Friday, June 12, 1903.
div.p: he Examiner Friday, June 12, 1903.
boat lay motionless on the glittering surface of the sea. ,

The next morning they tried to catCh some fish with a bent pin and a piece of red flannel from Hughes' shirt, but they caught nothing. By mid-day, however, a merciful breeze sprang up. They hoisted the sail and went spinning forward at the rate of seven knots an hour. Towards ' five o'clock the water began to be covered with dark patches, vary- ing in size from three inches to six feet in diameter. Tredegar feebly put his hand into the middle of one of them in the faint hope that it might be something edible. When he drew his fingers out they were alive with small grey spiders. He showed his hand to the others ; they regarded it apathetically and shook their heads. , ,

"The Chinese eat them, I believe," he said in a low voice. "At any rate they don't look any worse than snails." Then he-watched the hundreds of little legs moving in all directions, and hurriedly put his hand back into the water. Captain Williams burst into a laugh, and rising to his knees, looked anxiously towards the south. . _ _ . .

"Lana," he said hoarsely; "these things. mean land. Any fool can tell you that. Spiders ain't fishes, and they ain't birds either. It's land, you chicken hearted dogs. Why the [devil don't you dance and • sing, you swine ? "

And land it was. Before the sun set' that night a thin dark line rose from the horizon and raised itself slowly, into the sky as they Tinnier' thrnuah the water towarric it. The Idgfrays of light showed them a tall barrier of cliffs, barely two miles from their bows. They took down the sail and watched the land slowly merging into the darkness. It was hard for these starving neso tn bi.t.carnf-11, but Captain Willi 1; • •

sound or cry of a beast came from tht forests above. Save for the buzz of the countless wings and the ripple of the water at the bows of the boat, there was complete silence. In about a quarter of an hour the water- way turned abruptly to the left, the tall cliffs began to slip down to the level ground, and the eyes of the starving and thirsty men were gladdened with a sight that put fresh life into their weary hearts and bodies. The narrow channel suddenly widened out into a little circular lake, not more than two hundred yards in diameter. Its shores were of smooth white sand, littered and heaped pp with huge boulders, and a dozen little streams of clear :water struggled down through the dark masses of the rocks. A hundred yards from the edge of the lake the rock-strewn shore was circled by a belt of enormous trees, hung with tangled bunches of orchids and flaming creepers, and shutting out all view of the 'surrounding landscape with an im- penetrable wall of foliage. The men rowed the boat ashore with feeble strokes, and, dragging themselves to the nearest spring, drank deeply, and lay for a full hour in the shadow of a great rock. Then their thoughts turned to food.

They hastily improvised some fishing ap- paratus out of rope strands, bent nails, and pins, and a few pieces of coloured stuff. Then they pushed out the boat and tried their luck: TliPv were r...vard..(l b.vond their wildest hopes. Perhaps the fish- in these blue and shallow waters were more careless and frivolous than their fellows of the deep ocean. At any rate, the men caught two dozen in less than ten minutes. They were all of the same kind—long, thin, and silvery, with a few black spots on their backs. The men found them most excellent eating. They lach consumed one raw to stay the imme-

produced it, and they all drew lots for the prize. 'By an irony of fate Winkles won it. He realised his unworthiness, and, cutting the precious- thing in two, gave half back to Tredegar, and breaking up the other half with his fingers, filled a short• clay pipe with the fragments. Then the two smoked, and the others sat close to them to inhale as much of the fragrance as possible. They all talked - of their supper, which would probably in- clude meat; and Winkles ransacked his memory or his imagination for the most stirring anecdotes of his life, and in this way the afternoon rfassed pleasantly. At four o'clock they roused themselves to make some sort of shelter for the night. By fixing a sail across three large boulders they constructed a very decent imitation of a cave. The boulders enclosed three sides of it, and the canvas formed an excellent roof. in- structed by Winkles, they piled up a great heap of sticks and dead leaves in front of the entrance. He explained to them that it was necessary to light a fire at nightfall to scare off the wild beasts, and that all the best authorities were agreed on this point. By six o'clock they began to get rather anxious about their comrades. The island was so small that it would be almost impossible for any one to get lost in it. A man would only have to strike the coast-line and follow it round until he came to the creek. They had heard no sound of firing. They gave up all hopes I* meat for supper, and caught some more fish.

About eight o'clock the sun sank below the tops of the trees. The men cooked and ate their meal, and creeping into the shelter they had made for themselves, lit the fire. The opening of the little house faced the forest, and they hoped that the crackling pyramid of flame would serve as some guide to their companions. _ _

In a few- minutes darkness came down swiftly and suddenly, and they could see nothing but the glare of the firelight on the rocks and sand. There was complete silence. There were none of those strange sounds which come from a forest at night ; no cries of night birds or beasts of prey; not a snap- ping of a twig—nothing but silence. ....,,avvay-s talked cheerfully to each other, and peered but into the circle of light. From time to time one of them went to the entrance and shouted. The sound was echoed and re-echoed by the rocks, but there was no other answer. Then they drew happy pictures of their comrades sitting over a fire in the forest and cooking some succulent steaks from some most delicious animal.

Suddenly the silence was broken by the distant report of a rifle, and then by another report, and then by a long scream like the cry of a wounded beast. After that there was again silence. Dennis, Hughes, and the boy dozed off to sleep, and dreamt of roast meat for breakfast.

Tredegar alone could not close MS eyes He stretched his huge bulk on the sand) floor and stared hard into the darkness. But his thoughts were far away, and they would not let him sleep. He saw the black cliff-, of Cardiganshire, the low, stretch of yellow sand, and the great Cog. of Gogerddan, reaching to the circle of wooded mountains. He saw, too, the face of one he loved, more beautiful, as it seemed to him, than the face of an angel. He looked again into the dark eyes, filled with tears, as he had seen them last. He heard once more a low voice whis- pering to him, " I love you, Emrys, and will always love you. I will wait till you return to me I " Till he returned to her! He clenched his hands and laughed bitterly. Mavanwy Morgan might be an old woman bPfnre then. She might be dead. She

might even— at least she would be true. She would wait, wait, wait. Even the stern and grasping spirit of her father could not force her against her will. She would wait till her lover returned. And he would return—aye, and rich enough to pay off the mortgages on his estates and live in the home of his fathers. Tredegar's face grew stern and determined in the firelight, and the muscles stood out on his bare arms as he knotted his powerful fingers together. But in time Nature asserted her authority. Even this active mind could not fight against the exhaustion of the body. His head gradu- ally sank on his breast, and he fell asleep. When he woke the moon was high in the hr.-Ivens. The fire had died down to a few glowing ashes, but every detail of the shore was clearly cut and defiind in the moonlight. His companions still slept, and he could hear nothing but the sound of their breathing. He peered out towards the black wall of forest and listened attentively. He began to wonder why Williams and Morgan had not returned. He had half-hoped that the noise of their approach had roused him from his sleep. But he could hear nothing.

Then it struck him that the silence was not so complete as he fancied. No definite sound came to break the silence, but he began to fancy that the air was vibrating with .a long even murmur, 'so faint, and continuous as to be scarcely noticeable. He put the idea down to his imagination. A man who listens for sounds in the dead of night seldom fails to find them. After he had listened for two or three minutes a new fancy struck him. He began to imagine that the small stretch of sanu . . .

rocks that came within his range of visio. had, in some inexplicable manner, change. since he last saw it by daylight. It seeme in some way blurred—the white sand ha 4 grown darker, and the black rocks more grey Seeing that the effect of moonlight is t( heighten the lights and deepen the shadows this general grey effect was the more strange and startling'. He rubbed his --eyes, and observed everything carefully. Then, as he looked, something ran across his hand, an he saw it moving swiftly out of the shadow of the little house into the moonlight. It was about the size of a mouse, and of a grey colour. He could not see clearly what it was, but it appeared to have a large number of legs. He caught up a small stone from the sandy floor and hurled it with all his force at the flying patch of grey. Then a stranz.e thing happened.

The Whole extent ot beam and rocks seemed to suddenly quiver and move in the moon light, and millions of little grey things scuttled in all directions and piled themselves up in ridges and heaps in their fear and excitement. But in a few seconds they seemed to recover from their scare, 'and the whole mass began to-move slowly towards the forest. He woke his comrades with kicks and shouts, and flung a few sticks on the fire. In the blaze he saw two or three belated fugitives crawling across the sand. One of them got into the flames and frizzled there. He could see it quite plainly. It was an enormous spider, with a body an inch and a half it diameter, and legs not less than eight inches 'long. The other men were slow in waking, and by the time they were able to see or think clearly, there was nothing to be seen in the moonlight but black rocks and. white sand. The view had resumed its natural appear- ance. They plied Tredegar with wig Y questions. He told them what he had seen, 'and pointed to the little charred body in the fire. They believed then, and not one .of them closed their eyes again that night.

div.head: CHAPTER 11.
div.p: CHAPTER 11.
THE FOREST OF FEAR.

IN the' morning neither Captain Williams nor Morgan had returned, and their comrades resolved to go in search of them. After an early breakfast of fish, they walked up to the edge of the forest, and cutting *themselves some heavy sticks from the bushes, found the first mark that Morgan had " blazed " on the palm tree, and began to make their way through the undergrowth. It was not difficult to trace the path of the missing men. They had marked a tree every twenty yards, and even if they, had not done so it would have baen easy to see where they had forced their way through the den:. shrubs and creepers. They had, in fact, 011 out a clean path, and it was wonderful 110. much strength and energy had been diplaye by two men on the verge of starvation.
At first the men saw nothing to attr, their attention, unless indeed it was the ab
of all bird and animal life and the extraor profus'on of insects. But when th• \ penetrated to a distance of about 150 the whole wood seemed suakuly to mto animations

—lt is xio exaggt. ation to say that there were spiders everywhe3 e. E;ery leaf and frond trembled with their weight. The under- growth rustled as they moved through it in countless thousands. Hundreds scuttled away out of the path, and hundreds were trodden under foot. Their webs were woven from branch to branch and twig to twig till the very air seemed full of light network and quivering blots of grey. And everywhere winged insects flew, and struggled and died. It • was a horiible and disgusting sight. Before the searchers had gone another 150 yards their clothes were grey and shaggy with fine silken threads, and they had to brush insects from their hair' and eyes. The spiders were of all sizes, some two or three inches in diameter, and some scarcely bigger than the head of a pin. They appeared to be absolutely harmless. Hughes caught a large one in his hand, and it struggled like a rat, till he dropped it on the ground and crushed it with his heel. But it did not bite him.

Yet in spite of their harmlessness and their anxiety to escape, their very presence filled the men- with so great a horror that Tredegar had the utmost difficulty in persuading his .• companions to continue the search. How- ever, he drew so terrible a picture of the two missing men abandoned in that gruesome forest that the others were forced to proceed for very shame. In an hour's time they came to a spot where the trees were smaller and set farther apart. All the undergrowth had suddenly died away. In its place was a floor of hard earth and black rock. And still the spiders were every- where. It was now possible to see for some distance in every direction, and yet, strange to say, it was at , this point that the men lost the trail. They found the Mark of Morgan's knife on a tall mahogany tree, and after that were unable to find a single other sign of anyone having passed that way. It is true that they could no longer glean any information from the undergrowth, and that the earth and rock beneath their feet was so hard that it would not receive any impression of-a human foot. But it was. strange . that there was absolutely no further mark on the trees: They consulted together, and organised a definite plan of search. Tredegar remained by the mahogany tree, and the others Went out in three different directions through th.z forest. It was agreed that Tredegar should be a kind of landmark by which the others could retrace their footsteps to the path, and that he should shout at intervals to give them some idea of his whereabouts. In 'less than five minutes all three had passed out of Tregedar's sight, but he could still hear them tapping the trees with their sticks.

l'veiY three minutes by his watch he gave a loud and long call, and three distinct answers came back from the forest. Then, after a lapse of twenty minutes, there came only two answers to his cry. He waited for three minutes more, then called again and again in quick succession, but. still there were only two ,answers. Then he heard the- sound of someone running in the distance. It was Dennis, and he came panting through the trees with a white face.
" I've found sumniat, sir !" he cried "Come along me."

Tredegar -gave three sharp cries, the 'pre- arranged signal for all to return, and . then questioned Dennis as to what he had 'found. "The rifle," the man answered, huskily, " and blood. And there's summat else— God ,knows. what it is—l can't tell you, sir ; but it's More like a fishing net than anything." In a:few minutes Hughes came running up. He had not .seen or heard anything. But there was no sign of Winkles, and all thre. men ,kept shouting for ten minutes; but still he did not come. Then they decided to go and look at the timings Dennis had found, Marking every fifth tree as they went, and to return afterwards and wait till the boy turned up.

- They were not long in reaching the place indicated by Dennis. A rifle lay on the ground, and close by it an empty cartridge. Tredegar opened the breech and took out another cartridge, also empty. The weapon had been fired twice, and they called to mind the, two shots they had heard the night before. On the ground there were traces of blood and evidences of a struggle. The black rock was scratched, and the earth torn up into long ridges. A few yards away they found Morgan's knife. There was blood sticking to it, and some long yellowish hairs. Dennis picked up the rifle, and leading them farther into the forest, showed them a thing which might well set the brain of any mail a-wondering. To all appearances it was a gigantic spider's Web. It was fifty feet in diameter, and every strand of it was an inch in thickness.

At the first glance, Tredegar's blood ran - cold. Was it possible that a spider of such .enormous proportions existed, and that Wil- liams and Morgan had been overpowered by its stupendous strength ? Then he examined it more carefully, and saw that each rope was composed, of thousands of thin glutinous strands woven and twisted together, and that the whole design had been constructed by ' knotting the ropes into the required pattern. The structure was stretched horizontally between several trees, and had the appear- ance of a gigantic hammock. " The work of a man ! " Tredegar said, turning to his comrades. The others examined the thing, and nodded their heads.

"Aye, sir," Dennis muttered. "No animal could make these knots. I should like to meet him." And he eyed the barrel of the rifle wist- fully. They had no, cartridges with them. "He must have been a strong fellow," Tredegar said. " The captain was no chicken —and he had a rifle, and Morgan could use a knife." .

They made their way back to the mahogany tree, and again called out for Winkles, all three of them together, so that the sound might carry farther. But there was no reply, though they waited there and con- tinued to call until they were faint with hunger and the sun was low in the heavens. "We will return," Tredegar said, in a low voice. "It is a horrible thing to leave the boy here in the darkness. But perhaps he has struck the coast, and he has only to follow it till--" he stopped suddenly. He remember- ed that they had argued in the same way about Captain Williams and Morgan, and that they had not returned.
They retraced their steps in silence, finding the marks on the trees with difficulty, for it was growing rapidly dark. At last, however, *"..• tin-or:en. all the lornr r, f',t
crawling and rustling fcrzst. at iui on to the shore.

They heaped up a pile of wood and lit it— they owed this much to Winkles, who would have insisted on its being done. Then they cooked some fish, ate a hearty supper in silence, and turned in for the night. They had a rifle with them now, and were not afraid of anything, either man or beast. Tredegar slipped a cartridge into the breech,. and laid it ready to his hand. It would go hard with anyone who attacked them in the night.

In the morning Winkles had not returned, and they went once more into the forest to look for their three missing comrades. They took the rifle with them and searched all day, but found nothing except spiders. An. acute sense of horror came over them, and a mad desire- to get out of the accursed place. They were all agreed on one point—none of them would enter the forest unless the other two went with him.

Yet even this precaution proved no safe- guard. Before another twenty-four hour had passed, Dennis had disappeared. He went, out one evening to fish on the far • side of the lake, and never returned. He haul taken the rifle .4ith him, and it was found' lying on a flat piece of rock. There was no sign of a struggle, and the cartridges was un- discharged. But there were curious foot- prints in the sand, like blurred impressions of human hands and feet, and there was also a long trail, as though some heavy body had. been dragged towards the forest. Tredegar and Hughes came to the con- clusion that their 'unfortunate comrade was undoubtedly dead. They had not been more than two hundred yards away froM him, and if he had been able to cry out they would have heard him. A great fear fell upon them, and so poTalysed their minds that they made no attempt at a rescue. They retired into their h-lter, and kept watch alternately until the
• b 1•41. -;-- of forest round their little bay seemed to each of thrin- like the yawning jaws of some terrible monstur waiting to swallow them up-in its depths. . _ .

But with the morning- light their courage returned to them. Tredegar rose to his feet and clenched his .great hands as he looked at the forest. He asked nothing better than 10 meet this thing face to face and feel it in his grasp, and strangle it or beat out its brains on the trunk of some tree. Two hours after sun- rise the two men entered the forest. Tre- degar carried the rifle under his arm, and twenty cartridges in his pocket. Hughes cut himself a bludgeon of ironwood sufficiently heavy to break a man's legs or batter in his skull.

They took a new route this time, and fol-- lowed the trail they had seen upon the beach— the footprints and the marks of something being dragged along the ground. This trail led them into a-more northerly direction than Captain Williams' path, and was an easy one• to follow. The undergrowth was crushed and broken, and the prints of the animal's feet. N ,re plainly visible from time to time. .Here and there the thick stem of a shrub was torn. in half, and Hughes thought he could dis- tinguish the mark of nails upon the bark. In' one place they found a long shred of cloth: upon a stout thorn, and recognised it as part. of Williams' coat. As on their last journey, the spiders were everywhere, but they scarcely. heeded them. Their minds were too intent on the matter they had in hand.. For two hours they followed the trail, and observed by reference to the compass, which was fortunately in their possession, that the path was sweeping round in a circular route towards the West. Then the wood began to grow more open, and in a few minutes they caught sight of a " blaze " upon a tree, anc found themselves upon their old track, close- to the place where they had waited in vain for Winkles to return.

They stood here a .little while, and gave several calls in the hope of hearing some answering voice; but there was no reply. Then they decided to make their way to the strange web they had discovered the day before. Tredegar held his rifle with both hands in order to raise it to his shoulder at a moment's notice.

Before they had gone very far, Hughes grasped him by the arm and pointed into the heart of the wood. They both stopped, and saw in the distance the strands of the giant web like fine threads against a clear piece of sky. In their centre was a large, dark patch with four arms or legs, like the figure of a man clinging to a wall; and, as they looked, it seemed as though the limbs moved. Nearer the edge of the web were four other patches, but these were motion- less. The sight reminded them horribly of a spider and four dead bluebottles. Tredegar raised the rifle quickly to his shoulder ; but Hughes cried out, and struck up the barrel. Wait, sir," he said hurriedly, "you don't know what it is yet".

"You are right," Tredegar replied, lower- ing the rifle. "We will get a little closer." And they crept from tree to tree as silently as they could. Before they had gone fifty yards, however, the object in the centre slid swiftly to the ground and disappeared. The others remained motionless. Tredegar r:ursed bitterly and fired into a mass of undergrowth beyond the web. Then he put his hand into his pocket for another cartridge. The pocket was empty and three of his fingers slid through a long tear in the cloth. It had probably been made by some thorn, and every single cartridge had dropped out. The two men went back several yards in the hope of finding at least one of the small metal tubes which meant so much to them, but they found nothing. Tredegar laughed as they retraced their steps. " It does not matter," he said ; "in fact it is a fairer game. I only ask to get within ar:n's length of the cre iture." _

In a fe-w minutes they came close to where the great web was strung up among the trees.. l'he huddled objects hung motionless in the sunlight. One of them was considerably smaller than the others. They were un- doubtedly human bodies. The backs were towlrds them, but the clothes were familiar. They rushed eagerly to the other side and looked on the faces. They were the faces of aptain Williams, arid Morgan, and Dennis, .1 nd the boy Winkles. Their hands and feet strapped close to the net with. pieces of
stotits and wiry creeper, and they were ti four dead.

rredegar and Hughes unfastened the bands ;Hence and lifted the bodies reverently to t earth. All their necks were broken, and ..r heads hung limply between their • lers. Round every throat were the •; blue marks of fingers or claws. (To be continued.)

div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
THE VISIT OF THE FRENCH PRESIDENT.

Preparations are going on apace for the visit of President Loubet, and it is now settled that it will take place early next month. He will arrive on July 6th, and stay for three days, making the French Embassy his headquarters. The programme of festivities, however, has not yet been finally settled, though in outline it is fairly well un- derstood. King Edward will himself meet the French Presi- dent at the station upon his arrival and wel- come him, and that same even- ing it is expect- ed that a State banquet will be held at Buck- ingham Palace. That is an as- sured item of the programme, as is a "return" M. PAUL CAMBON, State banquet, The French Ambassador. which will be
given by Monsr.

Loubet- to the King at the French Embassy. In addition, there will probably be a gala performance at the Opera. and a visit to the City, with possibly a luncheon at the Guildhall. There is talk of various other entertainments, but so far these are the only ones that are practically certain. During his three days' sojourn in London Presi- dent Loubf...t will be the guest of M. Paul Cambon, the French Ambassador, who is very popular and much respected in diplomatic circles; but, of course, the Embassy will be placed entirely at M. Loubet's disposal, and it is he who will do all the entertaining there. The vi4t of the King of Italy to France and England, which was to have immediately fol- lowed that of M..Loubet to London, has been postponed, and will not take place, until November.

div.head: "THE DREAM OF GERONTIUS."
div.p: "THE DREAM OF GERONTIUS."

On Saturday the first performance in London of Dr. Elgar's exposition of Cardinal Newman's poemu The Dream of Gerontius," was given in the new Roman Catholic Cathedral at West- minster. This cathedral is a magnificent building, and is now completed with the ex- ception of the decoration and finish of the walls and some of the altars. It was designed by the late Mr. J. F. Bentley, the well-known architect, and owes its existence mainly to the personal efforts of Cardinal Vaughan, the head of the Roman Catholic Church in England, who was unfortunately unable to be aresent at The Dream of Gerontius" on Saturday owing to ill health. He has been ill for some time, and, though- at the present moment better, it is feared that he will never be fit to do much more active work. A large and fashionable audience, however, gathered in his absence; and from every point of view the perform- ance was a great success. The object of it was CARDINAL VAI.ItHAN.

;WAR.' to raise fund.. to establish a school of music in connection with the new cathedral. The great edifice itself was cheerless in the extreme in view•of the lack of adornment, but otherwise the auspices were splendid. The composer. Dr. Elgar, himself conducted a magnificent orchestra, led by Mr. W. Frye Parker, and the North Staffordshire District Choral Society supplied the chorus. They were excellent throughout, and shone especially in the chorus of "Demons." The exacting music for " Ger- ontius " was sung by Dr. Ludwig Wullner, and Nlr. Ffrangcon Davies sang the P.riest music in the first part and that of the "Angel of Agony" in the second. Miss Muriel Foster sang the mezzo-soprano " Ang, 4 " music. The music, .however. did not seem entirely con- genial to the solo singers. aid it was rather in the choral and orchestral portions that it Lame out most biillianilv. However, upon the whole the performance was a splendid succeis.

div.head: SIR ALLEN SARLE. .
div.p: SIR ALLEN SARLE. .

The death was announced at the end of last tveek of Sir Allen Lanyon Sane, the man who, perhaps more than any other had to do with the development of the London and South Coast system of railways. At the age of twenty- one he entered the company's service, when it -was compara- tively speaking in its infancy, and he was general manager of the railway until his retire- ment a few years backs When he became a clerk in the accountants' office in 1849 there was no such place as Victoria Stationa There was cer- tainly a line to Brighton, but the rest of the coast was prac- tically unde- veloped It was THE LATE SIR ALLEN under his keen SARLE. eye that Worth- ing, Hastings, An Rminent Railway Magnate. Eas tbour ae,

Bognor, Bexhill, Littlehampton, and St. Leonards were changed from little fishing villages into prosperous water- ing places. With regard to them he followed out a consistent policy of development; by supplying places for people to go to within easy access of town he provided passengers and revenues for his company. The NeWhaven- Dieppe route was another of his additions to the railway. He was, indeed, a pioneer of cheap railway transit, doing away with high fares on " express " trains and encouraging people_ to

travel by offering cheap return tickets arid fast excursions. Practically the only place on the line that he scrupulously left undeveloped, owing to a limited train service, was Banstead in Surrey, where he himself lived and died in the heart of the beautiful " down" country. Having a "special" always at his disposal, it was not so much inconvenience to him as to the other dwellers in Banstead. But people were not encouraged to live in that lovely spot by the inducement of railway facilities. ,The son of a Falmouth lawyer, Sir Allen Sane was .born in 1828 in Orkney and educated in Edinburgh.

div.head: TH2 ICING AND QUEEN AT ST. PAUL'S CATHEDRA:
div.p: TH2 ICING AND QUEEN AT ST. PAUL'S CATHEDRA:

On Sunday King Edward accompanied by the Queen paid hi., third visit to St. Paul's Cathedral within twelve months, and the first of a series of four visits to the City within the next few months. The object of the visit was to be present at the Hospital Sunday service in the Cathedral, and to aid the fund as far as possible by Royal patronage. It is next Sun- day, not last Sunday, wych is actually Hos- pital Sunday in the metropolis: but, as His Majesty will be out of town with the Court at Windsor next week-end, the service was held 'last Sunday at his special desire, so that he -might be present in person. King Edward has .always shown himself particularly interested in all matters to do with hospital work, and -was, it will always be remembered, the origi- nator of King Edward's Hospital Fund, which is so invaluable to those voluntarily-supported 'institutions. Last year £62,000 was raised by 'Hosp;tal Sunday contributions, and this year ,a great effort is being made to top Lloo,ooo. Mr. George Herring, the well-known philanthro- pist, has again promised to increase the fund 'by a quarter of whatever is publicly subscribed, a truly magnificent promise. By the King's re- quest Sunday's ceremony was kept as simple as -possible. Their Majesties drove in a four-
A QUAINT CEREMONY: THE PRESENTATION TO THE KING OF THE STATE SWORD BY TIIE LORD MAYOR OF LONDON.

t‘orse carriage via The Mall, Whitehall, and the Embailkment to St. Paul's; and the only f imal piece of pomp on the route was the presentation of the pearl state sword of the City by the Lord Mayor—with whom were the Sheriffs and other civic dignitaries—at the City boundary on the Embankment. This picturesque ceremony is one which tradition enforces every time a ruling sovereign visits the City, and the King himself is the last person who would wish it dispensed with. An inclined platform was put -up across the steps ,of the Cathedral, as it always gives the King slight troitible to a-cend steps since the acci- dent to ¶iis knee, and the aisle was lined by two hundred nurses from the leading London hospitals. Their Majesties obcupied chairs under the dome, with the other members of the Roya' family grouped round them. The service follemed the usual:, lines of " EvPn- song," and the sermon was preached by the Bishop of Stepney. At its conclusion the royal party left the Cathedral by the west door and drove back' to Buckingham Palace by the same route. Their reception was, as always, most cordial, and a large crowd lined the streets to watch the royal procession in a good cau-s.
THE RE-OPENING OF PARLIAMENT. Parliament reopened on Monday: and _there

is every promise of a more than usually lively session. To begin with, Mr. Chamberlain's • new fiscal policy sprung upon his supporters as well as the Opposition just before the House of Commons rose for its Whitsun vacation, has already been the sub- ject of conten- tion and dis- cussion; and there is little doubt that it will be well thrashed out before the ses- sion closes, as everybody is deeply inter- ested in it. This, more than any- thing else at the moment, looks like giving the Government their hardest nut to crack. Besides this im- portant ques- tion, the Gover- n JOHN REDMOND, . ment have on Leader of the Irish Nationalist their hands two Party. bills of unusual weight, which are likely to excite considerable opposition Irom various sections in the House. These are the Education Bill for London, and the Irish Land Bill. The former has had every step of its progress fought tooth and nail by the Liberals, aided by a few discontented ad- herents of the Government, and the agitation seems to have grown of late rather than de- creased. With regard to the latter, the Govern- ment in the first place have at its back a useful nucleus of the eighty odd votes of the Irish party, which used to be regularly registered against them on a decision, and an urgent whip has been sent round to them by Mr. John Redmond, their leader in the House of Commons, requesting their attendance regularly through- out the session from Monday onwards. They 'themselves have certain amendments to pro- pose. to Mr. Wyndham's Land Bill, but in the main they accept it with satisfaction, and are determined that, if they can help it, no catch- vote on any other question shall get the present Administration out of power before it has become law. The majority of the opposition in this case emanates from the Unionist benches, where feeling runs high on the question both of equity, and of the advisability of the Bill. Thus all round a particularly interest- ing session is promised.
M.P.

div.head: HIS MAJESTY'S NEW LAUNCH.
div.p: HIS MAJESTY'S NEW LAUNCH.

. It is some considerable time since much has ,been seen of Royalty on the river, which is such .a popular resort of Londoners; hence His Majesty's presence a few days ago with a bachelor party in the new royal launch; was hailed with enthusiasm by the crowd in boats, punts, and canoes. The King, who seemed to be out for a holiday as much as any of his loyal subjects, appeared in the most g9ial of tempers,
THE KING'S NEW LAUNCH.

and thoroughly enjoyed the informal reception .which was accorded to him in the teeth of •etiquette. He was greeted and cheered on all sides, " For he's a jolly good fellow" being sung by some of the mcst enthusiastic, and he con- stantly bowed and raised his hat in response to the spontaneous outburst. It is expected that be will now frequently make use of his new launch. It was built for His Majesty by Messrs. Tom Tagg & Son, and is worked by a petrol motor of the latest type. It is a handsome .craft, English-made throughout, and built to hold ten persons. It is 33 ft. 6 ins. long, and 61t. .n the beam. It is built in three skins, cedar, and mahogany, and with the exterior en- imelled white above and green below the water- mark. It is upholstered in blue leather, and the interior is lined with polished walnut and ash. Over it, supported on brass stanchions, Is a cream-coloured awning with a silk fringe and tassels. The engines are by Messrs.
Thorneycroft, and are very powerful, bemg capable of a speed of twelve to fifteen miles an hours The launch is housed in the royal boat-house in Datchet.

The Examiner, Friday, June 12, 1903.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Confirmation at Holy Trinity Church.

On Monday afternoon the Suffragan Bishop of Liver- pool (Canon Royston) held a confirmation service at Holy Trinity Church, Warrington, when sixty candi- dates from the parish were presented. The Bishop delivered two helpful addresses.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. Mr. B. Farrar presided at the meeting of this Society on Sunday afternoon. He announced that as secretary of the Society he had received letters from Mr. J. J. Evans and Mr. John Boyle acknowledging the messages of condolence which the Society had sent.—Mr. C. Booth, of Ancoats, Manchester, delivered an address upon "Duties "—duties to their dear ones; duties to employers and duties to their fellow-men. He pro- ceeded to refer to the good work which was being carried on in the lodging houses of Ancoats.—Mr. A. Downes and Mr. J. Owen also took part in the meeting.

div.head: Bold Street Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bold Street Wesleyan Church.

There were large congregations at this church on Sunday when the Sunday school anniversary services were held, and the Rev. J. Howell Jones, of Bolton, and formerly of the Warrington circuit, preached. The musical plrt of the services was very enjoyable, the choir rendering special hymns and anthems at both services. In the morning Mrs. Booth interpreted the solo "Thou mighty King," and in the evening Mr. E. H. Pearce sang Arm, arm, ye brave." A spe-cial ser- vice was held in the afternoon. Mr. Henshall presided, and an address was delivered by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees. The collections for the day amounted to about £45.

div.head: Church and Socialism.
div.p: The Church and Socialism.

The Rev. H. Dunnico preaching at the Baptist Church, Golborne-street, on Sunday evening, observed that though there might be false systems of socialism, socialism itself should not therefore be condemned. Socialism had come to stay, and it was the duty of the Church to take up the subject. Socialism required that a man who wished to work should be able to do so that he should not be overworked, that he should be well housed, well fed and well clothed, and have his share in all the privileges of the community. The Church had so far ignored its claims, and the only way to truly serve one's fellowmen was by first of all being consecrated to Jesus Christ, for love to God resulted in love to one's neighbour.

Church of the Sacred Heart. The Rev. Father McHale, S.J. Principal of St. Francis Xavier's College, Liverpool, preached the annual sermons on behalf of the schools in connection with the above Church on Sunday. The services were well attended. In the morning solemn high Mass was celebrated, the music being Farmer's Mass in B flat. At the offertory Miss S. Eastens gave a very effective interpretation of jZingarelli's " Ecce Panis." In the course of his sermon, Father Mc Hale made *n a.)peal on behalf of the schools. He said that in the past they had built schools and made tremendous sacrifices for their children, bemuse they valued their faith. They knew how much depended upon the children's early years, and had made sacrifices cheerfully. The necessity for that was now practically removed, but the new Act had not done all. They would still have new gchools to build if necessary, and would have to clear off all the debts •on the existing premises. He was there that day to ask their assistance in wiping off the debt on their own schools.—ln the evening Father McHale spoke upon Catholic devotion to the Sacred Heart. Choral devotions to the Sacred Heart were sung by the choir after the sermon. "There is a green hill " was sung by Mr. Percy George (baritone) in a feeling manner during Benediction. Nenkomm's "Ave Maria" was rendered by the Misses Fairclough and Richardson,and Mr. J. Gibbins (bass). The choir was under the con- ductorship of Mr. J. Gibbins, and Mr. J. Broadhurst pre- sided at the organ with ability.

Walkers Walking to Warrington. Atherton Parish Church House officials have arranged a walk open to residents within a four miles' radius to-day to Warrington and back, a distance of 25 miles. Medals are being given to the first four. The Leigh hairdressers are also having a long-dis- tance walk in a fortnight. Mr. Byerley's Will.

Mr. 'lobed-. Byerley, retired civil servant, who died at his residence, Warrington, on the 30th April appointed as his executor his son, Mr. Morris Grant Byerley, veterinary surgeon, by whom the estate has ben returned of the value of £2,858, including net personality, £2,757.

COMMERCIAL FAlLURES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the number of New Bankruptcy Proceedings in England and Wales glzetted during the week ending June was 53. The number in the cor- responding week of last year was 91, showing a decrease of 38, being a net decrease in 1903, to date, of 38.

div.head: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.
div.p: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.
This Council held its monthly meeting in Bold-street Wesleyan School on Wednesday evening, Mr. O. Buck- ley presiding in the absence of the President. There was a fair attendance of delegates.
CORPORATION CONTRACTS.—IS THE PAIR WAGE CLAUSE BEING ADHERED To? .

The SECRETARY submitted correspondence in regard to the contract for the Corporation Tramwaymen's clothing. He said it had taken some time to ascertain where the clothing was made. He had been told on several occasions by the Town Clerk and members of the Town Council that it was for the Trades Council to show, if they were not satisfied, that the work was not being done in accordance with the spirit of the fair con- tracts clause of the Tawn Council. It seemed to him that the Town Counoil never tookany steps to ascertain what the conditians observed by the contracting firms were. They accepted the tenders which they thought fit with- out making the full inquiries which the Trade Unionists thought were necessary. It therefore devolved upon him to obtain information,and after ascertaining which firm supplied the clothing, he wrote to Mr. McDonald, secretary to the London Trades Council, inquiring as to the conditions of labour adopted by them. He received a reply stating that the firm did not comply with the conditions recognized by the London Master Tailors' almociation and the members of the Amalgamated gociety of Tailors. The system of work was that of sub-division of labour, which in itself might not be objectionable bat when it was associated with piece work and at prices about 50 per cent. below the standard time then they considered it sweating and so dubbed the firm a sweating one. He had also received a letter from the Amalgamtted Union of Clothiers' Operatives which stated that the firm was a fair shop and paid the rate of wage laid down by their Society. The SECRETARY said it was for the Council to say whether they were satisfied that the firm was one which might be said to adhere to the spirit of the fair contracts clause. He was anxious that the matter should be brought forward in order to let the Town Council see thAt they were investigating all the con- tracts Oven out by the Corporation. Mr. H NiBLETT moved that the Secretary be instructed to ascertain whether the firm employed female labour and if so at what rate it was paid for. Mr. BALL seconded and the proposition was agreed to

div.head: LABOUR REPRES'ENrATIONPROPOSED DENIONSTRATION,
div.p: LABOUR REPRES'ENrATIONPROPOSED DENIONSTRATION,

The SECRETA.RY stated that at the last meeting of the Council they discussed at some length the ad- visability of holding a demonstration in the autumn and the consideration of the matter was adjourned for I a month. Since the meeting he had received a letter I from the Secretary of the Labour Representation Com- mittee inviting the Council to co-operate with the committee in holding a labour demonstration in Parr I Hall. It was suggested that the meeting should be held in September or October. It would be advisable, even on economical grounds, to co-operate with the Labour Representation Committee. The question of contesting municipal elections was discussed but the further con- sideration of thematter was adjourned owing to the small attendance of delegates. Another matter intro- duced was the advisability or otherwise of taking steps to secure a labour candidate for the Warrington con- stituency. It was stated that the present member, with all due respect to him as a gentleman, did not voice the opinions of the working , classes of Warrington. Seeing that the movement for Independent labour representation was growing so strongly throughout England and Scotland, the Com- mittee thought it was time Warrington began to discuss the question, if it were not actually decided to select a candidate. This question was also adjourned until the Inet meeting. There were now twelve or thirteen societies affiliated with the Committee, hut only 600 of th 3 3,000 trade unionists in the town were represented. That did not speak very well for the enthusiasm of Warrington trade unionists in the matter of representa- tion.

After some discussion, it was decided on the proposi- tion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. FERGUSON, to co-operate with the Committee in holding the demons- tration, and Messrs. Malone, Podmore and Potts were appointed a sub-committee to confer with a sub-com- m'ttee of the Labour Representation Committee as to the arrangements. THE WIREWORKERS' DISPUTE. CONCILIATION BOARD ASKED TO TAKE ACTION.

Mr. WHITTAKER informed the Council that the wire workers' dispute remained unsettled,in fact they did not seem to be in any better position than they were when they came out. This was the seventeenth week of the strike. About three weeks ago they received informa- tion that one firm was really on its beam ends, but un- fortunat.ly two of their men went in and the dispute had thus been prolonged. Mr. MALONE s,Lid he thought a Conciliation Board was appointed. Was it dead? The SECRETARY said he had mentioned the matter to Mr. Plinston who represented the Council on the Board and was also the secretary. He suggested that it was time something was being done or the Conciliation Board would become nothing less than a laughing stock. If any member was to blame it was the secre- tary and he was sorry Mr. Plinston was not present. He believed it said in the rules that as soon as it came to the knowledge of the secretary that a dispute was pend- ing he should write to the employers and employs on the matter. The Trades Council and Chamber of Com- merce went to considerable trouble to form a Concilia- tion Board and now it had an opportunity of doing some work.

Mr. FERGUSON moved that the Seoretary should write to Mr. Plinston expressing the opinion that the Con- ciliation Board should offer its services to the parties in dispute. Mr. POWMORE said he was a member of the Concilia- tion Board. There had not been a meeting since the second revision of rules and he believed they came to the conclusion that it would he rather premature on the part of the Board to interfere until they were asked to do so. Unless Mr. Plinston had receivedanapplication from the parties concerned it would be out of place for the Board to take action. The Board could do nothing unless the parties were prepared to conciliate. Mr. HA.MBLETT moved an amendment that the wire weavers should be asked to approach the Conciliation Board. Mr. PLUMB took this view of the matter.

KENDRICK thought that when the Conciliation Board saw the time had arrived for intervention it was for them to approach the parties concerned. The CHAIRMAN was of the same opinion. The SECRETARY thought it was the duty of thi Secretary of the Board to write to the parties concerne immediately he knew that a dispute was penning. The Council were now discussing something they had no right to discuss as the matter ought to be left entirely with the Conciliation Board.
_ It was ultimately decided that the Secretary should write to Mr. Plinston asking him to communicate with the parties concerned.
A WORD TO IRREGULAR A'rrENDERS.

The CHAIRMAN referred to the irregular attendance on the p trt of some of the delegates, and said the rule was that if any delegite absented himself three times in succession the Secretary should write to his Society. The SECRETARY said he did not keep hard and fast to the rules, as some secretaries appeared to be rather annoyed when often written to on the matter. Some branches were so apathetic that he was afraid that if he wrote so often they would be deciding to withdraw.
THE INCREASE IN THE PRICa OF SHA.VING—HAIR- DRESSERS' ACTION SUPPORTED.

The SECRETARY read the letter from Mr. J. Podrnore, jun., which appeared it our columns last week in refer- ence to the advance in the price of shaving decided upon by the Hairdressers' Association. Mr. PODMORE asked the Connell to support the Association in the matter as the Council had a great deal of power in Warrington. The hairdressers stood in a unique position towards the other members of the Council who were their employers for the time being. He had found during his experience of work for labour that there was a number of people who were always prepared to throw stones at . Trade Unionists because they said they were not consistent. He had not the slightest doubt that the Trade Unionists of Warrington would be consistent in this matter and help the hairdressers to obtain the advance. He had spoken to many of the Association who were very pleased to find that the public were supporting them very heartily. In reply to a question as to whether all the members of the Association agreed to the extra charge, Mr. Podmore said there were two members of the Associa- tion who from the commencement had set their faces against the movement. The other members had tried every means in their power to win them over but midi- out avail. He was in hopes that in the future the two members would fall in with the new arrangement. The movement would mean an increase of membership of the Association as they were already making members of those who had not hitherto thrown in their lot with them. They were in hopes that in time all the hairdressers would be members. The increased vice would only mean an advance of about 20 per cent on a hairdressers total income. The SECRETARY moved that the President and Secre- tary be authorised to sign on behalf of the Council any appeal which the hairdressers might issue in regard to the advance. There was no Society affiliated with the Council which had assisted trade unionist§ more during the past five or six years ,than the hairdressers. They had hardly ever missed responding to any appeal which had been made to them. He believed this was the first occasion on which the hairdressers had appealed to the Council and he thought it was the duty of the Council to give them every possible assistance. Mr. BALL seconded and thought it was high time that the hairdressers advanced the price. Nearly all the towns in the Northern counties had adopted the advanced rate.
The motion was unanimously agreed to and the meet- ing con chided..

div.head: DEATH OF A FORMER WARRINGTON MINISTER.
div.p: DEATH OF A FORMER WARRINGTON MINISTER.

We regret to learn that the Rev. W. R. Parry, who was formerly minister in charge of Wycliffe Cock- hedge Mission, died on Sunday from paralysis of the brain. Mr. Parry was trained for the ministry at Lancashire College and during his stay in Warring- ton he made many friends. He left to take charge of the Congregational Church at Peasley Cross, St. Helens, from which he retired owing to ill-health. He leaves a widow and one child.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Newton Urban District Council was held on Monday, at the Totvn Hall. Earles- town. Mr. W. Collinwood presided, and there were also present Messrs. C. B. F. Borron, T. Ormand, J. W. ,Emmett, N. Siddeley, W. Gilmour, J. Simpson, G. F. Clarke, E. L. Bent, E. T. Evans, and Drs. Patterson and Latham, with C. Cole (clerk), R. T. Surtees (water in- spector), and A. Bowes (surveyor).

div.head: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
div.p: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the above committee it was resolved that a man be employed at the cemetery gates on Sun- day afternoons, for the purpose of preventing young children entering the grounds unless under the control of their parents.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF -GAS.
div.p: REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF -GAS.

At a meeting of the Gas Sub-committee it was re- solved that from and after Ist July next the charges for gas be reduced from 3s. 24. to 2s. 10d. per 1,000 cubic feet (less 6d. discount) and that the question of the reduction in the price of gas consumed throughi au- tomatic meters be considered 12 months hence, t ap- pearina that the increase in January, 1901, of 4d. did notaffect this class of consumers. The engineer was directed to report to the committee the amount of gas consumea for cooking and for motive power; the provision of boiling burners for all consumers ; the adoption of the hire system of stores. At a meeting of the Gas Committee it was proposed and seconded and an amendment that a 'reduction of 2d (or as near that amount as possible) per 1.000 cubic feet of gas be made in the price of gas supplied to consumers through ' the automatic meters. The amendment was lost. The chairman of the committee (Mr. W. Thompson) having stated that owing to indisposition he intended going away for same time, and that as he wished to be relieved of any responsibility as chairman he would like the committee to appoint another chairman in his place, it was resolved that the committee whilst regretting the cause of the chairman's proposed absence, was of the opinion that if he would retain the position of chairman the committee would oppoint a vice-chairman to act in his absence. Mr. Thompson having consented to the wishes of the committee, it was resolved that Mr. G. F. Clarke be appointed vice-chairman. The minutes after several amendments proposed by Dr. Latham and re- jected were carried.

div.head: OPEN-AIR SWIMMING BATH.
div.p: OPEN-AIR SWIMMING BATH.

The Surveyor also submitted his report upon the question of the conversion of" Thompson Pit" into an open-air swimming bath. It stated that the pit had the natural slops of the clay ground, and it would be neces- sary to clean out the existing mud from the bottom, and it was highly desirable that the whole of the pond should be lined with some hard material, such as setts, bricks or concrete. The Medical Officer thought that that lining should be dispensed with ;• at all events it was a preliminary scheme. Boarded fencing would be required all round the pond, dressing rooms, diving boards, rails and steps down into the water. The cost of the whole construction would be approxi- mately £550. The report further stated that an attendant would, be required, the owner of the land would have to be approached, and the question of the water supply would have to be con- sidered. Even if a natural supply could be arranged for, it was certain that the water supply of the town would have to be largely drawn on for.refilling the pond. He estimated the contents of the pond to be 755,000 gallons.' At the present price of water that would mean a cost of £36 e..?.ch time the pond was filled. Tt was resolved that the matter be deferred. The Sur- veyor also reported as to the, cost of street making, in which he stated that in his own opinion he was strongly in favour of the present style of sett paving as being the most suited to local requirements, and cheaper than any other system in the long run. If any other system cheaper in the first course was adopted, the cost of scavenging and maintenance would be increased. It was resolved that the recommendations embodied in ' such report be approved, and adopted. The report of the sub-committee appointed for the purpose of making arrangements for the improvement of the street corner iii Earle-street, was approved and adopted. It was decided to purchase a rain gauge to be fixed at the Cemetery.
THP RATES.

The Clerk submitted his estimates of expenditure at a meeting of the Finance Committee, when it was re- solved that the Council be recommended to levy a high- way rate of 7d. in the a general improvement rate of is. 2d. in the and a water rate of 3d. in the £.

div.head: FIRE BRIG ADV. AND AMBULANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FIRE BRIG ADV. AND AMBULANCE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this committee it was resolved that the Fire Brigade Superintendent be directed to ask the owners of the premises on which telephones are fixed to allow their telephone to be used in the case of fire and that when the consents are obtained lists of the telephones be printed and attached to the fire boxes and other places in the district. It was also resolved that a fire box be provided for the neighbourhood of the Common, also that a lamp he fixed outside the fire station. It was resolved that the request made by Mr. Surtees to he relieved of his duties of fire brigade superintendent be acceded to and that Mr. .T. T. Hoggard be appointed superintendent and Mr. E. P. Cleworth deputy superintendent and instructor to the brigade.

div.head: WATERWORKS-Z 1,300 TO BE SPENT,
div.p: THE WATERWORKS-Z 1,300 TO BE SPENT,

At a meeting of the Water Co7mmittee held that after- noon, it was resolved that a pump be purchased for pumping the clean water from the headings, at a cost of R 1,200, and arrangements be made with the Contractors to purchase the pump. Specifications for two houses at the pumping station were approved. The minutes were adopted. THE REQUIRED AWNING AT NEWTON STATION. Mr. Clarke asked if any reply had been received in answer to the letter on the above subject.—The Clerk said he wrote the General Manager of the London and North-Western Railway, cl,ho replied that the matter would receive attention.

Sequel to a Colliery Fatality."PM At the Warrington. County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C. Patrick Lawler, 52, Watery-lane, Sutton, - sued the Collins Green Colliery Company for compensation for the loss of his son who was killed at the colliery on Maroh nth—Mr. Riley, of St. Helens, represented the applicant and Mr. Edwin Place,of Liverpool, appeared for the respondents—Mr. Riley said the short issue of the case would practically be whether the. anplicant who was the father of a young man of about 20 or 21 who met his death in a way about which there was no dispute, was or was not, dependent upon the deceased, end if so to what extent—after hearing the evidence his Honour awarded applicant E. 60.

A HORSE'S STRANG F. T e.—Recently Mr. W. Walker, of the Abbey Farm. St. Bees, purchased a horse from a gentleman near Whitehaven. On Thursday morning the horse disappeared, and nothing was heard of it till Sunday, when news came to hand that Mr. Parker, of the Tarn Farm, Bootle, had found it on his premises. It had been proved that the horse made the whole journey of about 30 miles. keeping to the shore all the way. In order to accomplish this many stretches of water, the coast being very broken, must have been swum over. When found the animal was filthy, being covered with sand and seaweed. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
JUNE 12th, 1903.

Sir MICHAEL Mend- MR: CHAMBERLAIN BEACH made the DISATOWED. finest speech of his life on Tuesday ; and yet his momentous deliverance, in which those who heard it might have imagined themselves to be witnessing the birth throes of a new political era, was not the most important incident of a de- bate of which record will be kept as one of the turning points of English history. The actually most thrilling moments of the discussion must have been those in which the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER reading from a carefully prepared 'document, repudiated the policy of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. The proposals of the Colonial Secretary were not really before the House. The Speaker ruled, in advance of the debate on the Budget Bill, that what he called" the fiscal ques- tion" was not revelant to the Bill. But the Speaker himself obviously felt that, in the exist- lug condition of feeling, it would be impossible to suppress all allusion to the question which is at the moment occupying the minds of the whole 'Country. With an ex-Chancellor of the Ex- cilequer addressing the House for the first time 'lies his resignation, and on such a topic as the -B.lldget of the year; with the general ques- tlOn complicated by the revolutionary pro- Posals of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, clearly the best Policy for the Speaker was a charitable one. It was not an occasion for being too precise as to • the Parliamentary proprieties; and as a matte r of fact, though SIR MICHAEL HICKS-BEAC H was more than once called to order, he did in the long run contrive to express all that it was his purpose to say. There was a hint of very serious cleavages In the Cabinet in the speech of the former Chancellor of the Exchequer. The reasons for his resignation have never yet been fully disclosed; but they may without much difficulty be dis- cerned in the 351 m and measured and very serious harangue which he delivered to the House of Commons on Tuesday. He was evidently.% favour of a much greater reduction of expenditure than is Proposed in Mr. RITCHIE'S Budget, and there- fore in favour of a much larger reduction of taxa- tion. He would in particular have cut down the armament charges; but, as is easily read between the lines, Mr. BALFOUR sacrificed him to Mr. BRODRICK. The Premier no doubt felt the full 'severity of the declaration that "it is absolutely impossible for any CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER Whatever his desire for economy, really to check expenditure unless he has the firm, active, and continuous support of the Prime Minister.' This is really the strongest possible condemnation of a Prime Minister who, being neither industrious nor Well-informed, endeavours to steer a middle course between his colleagues, leaving them to them- selves as mach as possible, and giving his support to the most importunate, even though he may be the least able.

As te this policy of go-as-you-please, Which has now led the Government into the' Chamberlain morass, Sir MCCHAEL Mom-BEAGLE had BOMA exceedingly incisive things to say. He contended, 'reasonably enough, for the right of a Minister to Speak now and again without consulting his colleagues. "We must all blow oft steam some- times," he said; but blowing off steam is not the same thing as initiating new policies and putting forward unauthorised programmes. Various mem- bers of the Government, Mr. BaLrour. among them, have suggested that the Colonial Secretary, With the consent of his colleagues, was merely 'Putting forward a topic for discussion by the con- stituencies. At this point Sir MICHAEL HICKS- 13EACH draws the line'as to freedom of speech. The Position suggested by the Primellinister, he said, absolutely impossible. It is not fair. It is neither fair to the Government nor to the 'People. Though the matter could not then be discussed, he continued, it could not long be left without discussion. What was proposed was a vital change in the fiscal policy which had been accepted by the country.for fifty years, and which 'had even been accepted by the Tory party. The Promulgation of it had already performed some- thing like a miracle. It had united the Liberals; and it is dividing this side of the House," added the sic-CtiaircELLoit. '.of the EXCHEQUER. Why 'should not Ministers speak their minds ? The 'Policy of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN would do harm both to home and to Colonial interests. It would do more to disunite than to unite the Empire.

div.p: IR. CHAMBERLAIN AS HIS OWN CRITIC.

Interesting extracts have been published, from a speech delivered by the present Colonial Secretary in the House of Commons on the 12th August, 1881, in reply to a Fair Trade resolution moved on the same occasion by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. History, it is said, repeats itself; Mr. Chamberlain never does. He always contradicts himself. It is interesting, how- ever, to note that he and Mr. Ritchie are still at vari- ance on this question, the only difference being that the two statesmen have changed places,the Protectionist of 1881 having developed into a Cobdenite, while the Free Trader of that year, in growing older, has receded to the position formerly held by his antagonist. Among other things in that speech, he said :

England is of all countries the most vulnerable in this matter—that is to say that in spite of, or rather, I am inclined to say, in consequence of the Protectionist policy of foreign countries, we export a great deal more than we import in the way of manufactures. Therefore such a commercial war as the hon. member proposes would do us more harm than the foreigner, who might retaliate on our retaliation by prohibiting or still further in- creasing his duties on our goods, or even by putting a duty on the exports of articles which we do not produce for ourselves. Well, then, does anyone propose to put a duty on raw materials? Is it conceivable that we should ever be foolish enough to do away with the foundation of a great part of our trade—namely, the freedom with which we receive the raw material? Than he came to food taxation, and he asked— Is anyone bold enough to propose that we should put duties upon food? I can conceive it just possible, although it is very improbable, that, under the sting of great suffering and deceiyed by mis- representations, the working classes might be will- ing to try strange remedies, and might be foolish enough to submit for a time to a proposal to tax the food of the country, but one thing I am certain of. If this course is even taken, and if the depres- sion were to continue or to recur, it would be the signal for a state of things more dangerous and more disastrous than anything which has been seen in this country since the repeal of the corn law. With the growth of intelligence on the part of the working classes, and with the knowledge they now possess of their own power, the reaction against such a policy would be attended by consequences so serious that I do not like to contemplate them. A tax on food would mean a decline in wages. It would certainly involve a reduction in their productive value—the same amount of money would have a smaller purchasing power. It would mean more than this, for it would raise the price of every article produced in the United Kingdom, and it would indubitably bring about the loss of that gigantic export trade which the industry and energy of the country working un- der conditions of absolute freedom has been able to create.

Mr. Chamberlain must think the "growth of intel- ligence on the part of the working classes "has been a backward growth, or he would never come to them and ask them to adopt the course which he so strongly con- demned in 1881. But the most notable sentence in that, speech was this—"A tax on food would mean a decline in wages." That remains as true to-day as it was then. And yet, with this speech of his own on record against him, Mr. Chamberlain has the audacity to say a food tax to-day would raise wages as well as, by some sort of magic, provide Old-Age Pensions.
