to the House that he was abolishing the corn tax in the interests of Free Trade. He threw over Mr. CHAMBEEL. 4IN. He affirmed that he is a convinced Free Trader. He said that in his opinion no inquiry would be able to show that there is any pos*ible means of carrying out the policy of the Colonial Secretary. This Was a declaration of war, and it was a declaration that was prearranged. It places Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in a very singular position. He must leave the Government or remain in it for the purpose of compelling an.appeal to the country on his mon- strous proposals. This is not the first time that he has broken a party to pieces. He does not shrink from these undertakings. He rejoices in them indeed. But this time he appears to have made an extraordinary miscalculation. He may , break the Unionist party, but he will not gain his end.

The majority of people generally pay some attention to the weather forecasts published in the daily and evening papers, and by doing so obtain some fairly reliable information as to what may be expected atmospherically during the ensu- ing 24 hours. Tnose who studied the "Man- chester Evening News" on Wednesday must, how- ever, have received a shock, for the forecast, in clear, cold type, stabed as follows : "Eight easterly breezes; changeable, close, tlaund.iry." Fancy eight easterly breezes in one day; a fresh one every three hours! Ugh! How we shivered apprehensively. Thursday dawned and lo there was an easterly breeze). It was also colder, but whether this particular breeze was the first of the eight prophesied we could not deter- mine. Time failed to make us much gwiser, for the same breeze appeared to be blowing when darkness closed in upon the eventful day and we had observed nothing abnormal. The weather prophet of the " News " must have been joking, but if he is inclined that way again it is to be hoped that he will forecast sometbing pleasanter to contemplate than " eight easterly breezes." „al

Dr. Roberson Nicoll discusses, in the" British Weekly," an incidental question in regard to the Zollverein policy—its probable effect on the book trade. His inquiries and observations lead to the opinion that books are bought mainly by the middle classes, and particularly, perhaps, by the lower middle classes. Many of these persons re- :wive fixed salaries, whose purchasing power would be reduced by the change; and one of the plea- sures cut off would be the acquirement of a library. There is some ground for the argument in the depression which the book trade felt during the war. The professional writer would suffer, and fewer people would strive in the calling, which is already over- crowded. Carnegie libraries would not meet the situation. The irony of circumstances places these 1 braries in busy quarters among people who have the least time for reading ; and the country dis- tricts are neglected. To say that people read too much nowadays, and were better-informed in the old days, when they mastered one or two books, is to beg the question: The conditions of life— for citizens of a great Empire—require the elec- torate to have wider information than that, and it should be possible for every voter to have a small substantial library for reference. Further than that, every class should be able to learn something of the manners of the others by the aid of fiction, which opens up the different layers of society, and thus tends to correction as well as to the encouragement of charity.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
INJURY TO A SAILOR.

On Tuesday, John Stafford, a sailor, was working on a vessel lying at the Runcorn docks when he fell down the hold, sustaining serious injuries to his scalp and thigh. P.C. Rowland rendered first aid, the injured man afterwards being taken to the Cottage Hospital and attended by Dr. Cullen.

div.head: Ace [DENT TO A LABOURER.
div.p: Ace [DENT TO A LABOURER.

On Thursday morning a labourer named William Rowbottotn, 139, Surrey-street, working on the ship "Henry" sustained a severe injury to his back while following his employment. He was attended by Dr. Burke, locum totem, for Dr. McDougall and removed to his house on the ambulance. DEATH OP AN OLD RUNCORN TRADESMAN.

On Wednesday evening an old man aged 65 named Smith was found dead in the pantry of a, house in Queen-street. The deceased was at 'one time a leading Runcorn fishmonger but drink ruined him and for some time he had eked out a precarious existence by selling oranges. He was last seen alive on Tuesday night about seven o'clock. The house was in a wretchedly filthy condition. Smith had been living alone for some months. The Coroner has been notified. PETTY THEFTS AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday before Messrs. W. Timmins (in the chair) and Mr. E. Imison, Peter Rogers, Canal-street, was charged with having stolen on the 4th June two fowls the property of William Percival, Norton. The evidence showed that on the 3rd June the fowl cote was not locked and on the following morning the fowls were missing. P.C. Upton who received the news of the missing fowls went to the prisoner's house. He denied all knowledge of the missing fowls, but on the police officer looking in a pot on the fire one of the fowls was discovered, the feathers afterwards being found wrapped in paper. Prisoner wns next charged with stealing 1121 b of potatoes belonging to John Horton, Norton. Prisoner acknowledged the theft and was committed to gaol for two months in each ease.—At the same Court Frederick A.lillington of Northwich, was sent to gaol for three months for stealing on June 3rd 701 b of rope valued at 38. the property of Thomas Withy.

div.head: SHOCKING CHILD NE GLECT_ AT WIDNES.
div.p: SHOCKING CHILD NE GLECT_ AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Sessions, on Thursday, Catherine and John Roake, living in Brown-street, were charged with neglecting their family from 1895.—Mr. .1. W. Knowles, prosecuting on behalf of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, stated that this family had been under the society's supervision for some years. On the 28th of last month Inspector Hob- den visited the house where defendants were lodging. The children were in a shocking condition, filthily dirty, and bitten severely with vermin. They were apparently starving. The husband was away in , St. Helens, but sent his wife barely enough money to pay her lodgings, leaving little or nothing for food. The sleeping accommodation was only a straw mattress ,on the floor, with only one covering. On the 9th of the presentmonth he again visited the house, and notwith- standing the caution administered on the previous visit I things went from bad to worse, necessitating the arrest lof the woman and the apprehension of the man in St. Helens on Wednesday.—lnspector Hobden, Police- constable Greenhalgh, and Police-constable Cummings, ' all gave testimony of the parents' shocking behaviour.— The bench characterised the case as a bad one,and sent both to prison for three months.

div.head: RUNCORN SONS OP TEMPF:RA.NCE.
div.p: RUNCORN SONS OP TEMPF:RA.NCE.

The usual fortnightly meeting, of the division was held on Saturday evening inbGreenway-road School- room, Runcorn. After the ordinary business, Bro. George Powell, W.P., gave a very interesting report of his visit to the National Division Session, which was held at Huddersfield,in Whit-week.He was atcompanied by Bre.Thomas Whyte and W. Patron,both being repre- sentatives of the Runcorn Division. Bro. William Glead- hill, of Hull, on becoming chief officer of the order at the commencement of the new century had urged the National Division and the order to make special efforts during his term (two years) to make a record increase of 10,000. This had been accomplished, the result being 10,021. The total number of adult meinhers was now 59,308, the average sickness experience was 7.9 days per member, and the mortality 5.8 per thousand members, the capital being over a quarter of a million —a gain of over £20,000 for the year. Thirty-eight new adult branches had been established during the year. There were 530 cadet (juvenile) branches with 33,381 members, their funds being in a very flourishing condition.—Bro. Powell said that the conference was marked by great enthusiasm, there being animated dis- cussions on the Friendly Societies' Old-Age Pension Scheme and other matters connected with the order in- cluding a new scheme for accident assurance and matters connected with temperance legislation. The hospitality extended to the delegates was all that could be desired, and they had been entertained by Sir Thomas Brooke, Bart., and others, as well as by members of the order. Bro. William Scott, of Newcastle, was elected chief officer of the order (Most Worthy Patriarch), and Bro. Walter Davies- of Manchester, vice-president (Most Worthy Associate). Bro.WilliamWightman, of London, is the permanent secretary (Most Worthy Scribe), Bro. Thomas Whyte also spoke on the report, emphasizing all that had been said by Bro. Powell. A division followed, much gratification being expressed by the brethren at the excellent result of the year's work. The thanks of the division were tendered to Bros. Powell and Whyte, for their report, on the motion of Bro. T. J. Holt, seconded by Bro. Thomas Clarke.

div.head: FRODSHAM IN 1808. A Spring Used as a Cold Bath.
div.p: FRODSHAM IN 1808. A Spring Used as a Cold Bath.

Last week we gave extracts from a topographical dictionary compiled in 1808, showing how Warrington and Newton appeared nearly a hundred years ago. The following information from the same authority relating to Frodsham will doubtless be read with interest :

Fnonsium, a market town and parish in the hundred of Eddisbury. Chester, on the banks of the river Weaver, 10 miles from Chester and 193 from London; containing 272 houses and 1,551. inhabitant.. Its name is supposed to be derived front a ford over the river before the erection of La present stone bridge. The town consists of two main streets, spacious and well paved, intersecting Poach other at right angles about the middle of the town. The church stands on a lofty hill, at the ex- tremity of one of these streets, and is a very handsome ancient building, repaired and beautified in 1790. The town has a well-endowed free school. The circumfer- ence of the, parish is about 31 miles, bordering on the forest of De In Mere, and containing about 10 small villages, besides the market town. The principal em- ployment of the inhabitants is the refining of salt, and in a small manufacture of cotton. A graving dock and yard have been lately erected here, for building and re- pairing of vessels. Atthe west end of the town formerly stood Maurice Castle, the seat of the earls Rivers. On Beacon Hill, above the town, was formerly placed above the town, was formerly place a signal-beacon. This hill is now out out into walks, having a gradual ascent to the summit, whence there is a charming pro- spect of the surrounding country, intersected by the rivers Mersey and Weaver, and the navigable canal. The town is well supplied with water from several excellent springs, one of which discharges 1,700 gallons in a minute, and is used as a cold bath. The market is on Thursday; and fairs on the 15th May and 21st August for cattle. The-living is a vicarage, value £23 13s. 11d.' in the patronage of the dean and canons of Christ Church, Oxford. When this dictionary was compiled Widnes had only 219 houses and 1,063 inhabitants, and Runcorn 220 houses and 1,379 inhabitants.

PASSIVE RESISTANCE. AN EARLBSTOWN RESISTER. Mr. George Cook writes from Newton-le-Willows : At the Earlestown Primitive Methodist quarterly meeting, held on Saturday last, a resolution was unanimously passed approving of my refusal to pay the education rate, and pledging to stand by me in all the consequences of my refusal. Everyone present expressed his willingness to enrol himself in a citizen league if one were formed, and early steps will be taken to form such a league for Earlestown and the district. I am now awaiting a summons to appear before the magistrates for non-payment of the education rate. WHAT PASSIVE RESISTERS STAND FOR. ADDRESS AT WARRINGTON.

Mr. Andrew Scriven, of Warrington, delivered an I address on " Passive Resistance" at the meeting of the P.S.A. Society held in the Methodist Free Church, Buckley-street, on Sunday. He based his address on the words :—" For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities,against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world,against spiritual weakness in high places." There were great objections to the Education Bill of 1902, he said, from a Noncon- formist standpoint, because the Bill tended to give greater facilities for the teaching of those things which they believedwere diametrically opposed to true Chris- tianity. It was through those objections that Noncon- formists had formed a "Passive Resistance League," which was composed of those who refused to pay the Education rate, because they conscientiously objected to the bad principles of the Bill. In consequence of this attitude on the part of the "Resisters," their goods would be seized by the authorities to pay the rates. They would allow their goods to be taken from them: but they would not submit to this, in their opinion, repugnant measure. Of course the enemies of the Evangelical Churches had done their utmost to turn the "Resisters" from their decision,by offering them sugar- coated pills, whichthey tendered in the form of "Now this Bill is solely in the interests of the education of the rising generation." Needless to say they had smelled a "rat" and they would not be convinced of the sincerity of their having "the deepest interests of the educational needs of the children" at heart. It had been argued that Nonconformists should be the first to ' obey the law; but he wished to remind them that the law was of man, not of God, and they refused to submit to it on the grounds of its non-compliance with the law of God. As Nonconformists, they could only obey the law of man in so far as it agreed with the law of God. They had taken their standard of God, and they emphati- cally refused to accept the standard of man. Withall due deference to those in authority, they, as "Re- sisters," could not, and would not, submit to that law which gave greater power for the teaching of those things which were obnoxious to the fine susceptibilities of the inner life of Nonconformity. It was of no con- sequence to them whether the Bill was passed by a large majority or not, because they believed that a man must obey the voice of conscience. llt was suggested by many that those men who had adopted "Passive Resistance" were endeavouring to , make martyrs of themselves. He could assure them that the "Resisters" were courting no such position; but ,he felt confident that if occasion did arise there were thousands of the bravest sons of Nonconformity who were both ready and willing to sacrifice not only their goods and chattels, but themselves, for conscience's sake." Some people, too, insinuated that the "Resisters" objected to the rate, in order to save them 2a. d. That was a perfectly ridiculous, and absolutely monstrous, charge to make. Anyone with a grain of commonsense knew very well that it would cost the "Resisters " a great deal more, owing to the extra charges in levying distraint. They had, however, counted the cost, and were prepared to make the sacrifice. He hoped they, as P.S.A. brethren,, would i not be like the Levite n the story of the good Samaritan, who, having looked at the wounded Jew's condition, passed by on the other side. They must support the 'Resisters" by their earnest prayers and loving sympathy. A great crisis had come to test their real worth, and it behoved them to be up and doing. He was sorry to warn them that there were traitors in the camp of Nonconformity in this town, men who had given their pledge to support this "Passive Resist- ance "movement, who, when the time came for them to show their sincerity, withdrew those pledges rather than" face the music." Suchmen as those, who would sink their honest convictions for the sake of the majority, were, in his opinion, contemptible. The Chair was occupied by Mr. William Smith, Mr. Critchley sang two solos entitled The Watchers "and "Dream of Paradise," and Mr. Pemberton sang "Beauti- ful Bells." Mr. A. E,Tr6w was the accompanist. A JUDGE JOINS THE RANKS.

Judge Willis, K.C., of the Norfolk County Court, was the principal speaker on Wednesday night at a meeting held at King's Lynn, in connection with the Norfolk Baptist Association. Amid great enthusiasm on the part of the delegates he declared himself an adherent of the policy of passive resistance.

div.head: CHESHIRE.
div.p: CHESHIRE.

A passive resistance society has been organised in Crewe and district in connection with the education rate. Ministerial ministers of the Free Church Council will resist payment, and at present there are about 100 objectors. A memorial is being adopted for presenta- tion to the authorities, asking that in the demand for rates the sum required for education purposes shall be specially indicated. •

WARRINGTON. Shepherds A.M.C. and Old Age Pensions. On the resumption of the A.M.C. of the Loyal Order of Shepherds, on Saturday, at Chorley, the con- sider&tion of a scheme of old-age pensions, submitted by the Committee of the National Conference of Friendly Societies, elicited some singular views.— Bro. Abbot (valuer) moved "That, inasmuch as the Committee of the National Conference in preparing their pension scheme have violated the forms of refer- enre on which they were instructed, and having prepared a scheme more calculated to endow the wealthy than to relieve old-age poverty, this annual meeting decline to approve the scheme." Bro. Abbot strongly denounced the scheme, remarking that every man who aided in drafting the scheme came under the category of men who were legislating for themselves, and not for poor men who were unable to work from old age. He objected to the country being taxed for the benefit of wealthy people who, thus helped, would diminish the wages of the workers.— Bro. Saunders (Bristol) moved an amendment that the conferende express approval of the old age pension scheme.—Bro. Ellis (Bristol) seconded the amend- ment, which was carried by 71 votes to 30, amid applause.—Salaries and honorariums were voted, and thanks accorded to the Mayor and others, after which Bro. George Rise (Potteries) was installed Chief Shepherd, and the conference concluded. ,

div.head: SUCCESSFUL FUNCTION AT THE
div.p: SUCCESSFUL FUNCTION AT THE
TOWN HALL.

There was a cordial response to the invitations issued by the Mayor and Mayoress (Mr. and Mrs. J. Charlton Parr) for Tuesday's "At Home" at the Town Hall and the function proved a highly successful and enjoyable one. About 900 invitations had been sent out and during the afternoon there was a constant stream of visitors. With their usual regard for the comfort of their guests, the Mayor and Mayoress decided upon an acceptable diversion from the usual course of events at such functions, a garden party being held on the lawn behind the 'Town Hall. The guests were received in the Council Chamber, the Mayor wearing his chain of office and the Mayoress carrying a lovely bouquet of orchids. They then passed down the steps to the lawn and whiled away a pleasant hour under most congenial circumstances. Although the day was not very bright there were occasional flashes of sunshine, and it was very enjoyable to saunter about the gardens, the beauties of which are at present enhanced by the fine display of rhododendrons. . Those who desired to in- dulge in croquet and "putting" on minature golf links were afforded ample facilities for doing so, and [ the games found many enthusiastic exponents. ' Afternoon tea was served on the lawn, as I well as in the Town Hall, the catering being carried out by Mr. and Mrs. Powys in their best style. One of the small arbours to the right of the lawn had been prettily draped and here ices could be obtained. The Misses Parr were assiduous in their attention to the guests, and did all in their power to ensure the success of the "At Home." There was general regret that the Town. Clerk and Boro' Treasurer were prevented from attending by indispositions. The Band'of the Ist Volunteer Battalion Prince of IWales' Volunteers (South Lancashire Regiment) was in attendance-and under the conductorship of Mr. J. T. Richardson played the following selections in ad- mirable style : I March "The Crusader" Sousa 2 Selection " Faust " Gounod 3 Intermezzo " Ilypatia " Hume 4 Fantasia " Darkies' Jubilee" Newton 5 March " Land of my Home" Brunt 6 Selection "Sullivan's Operas" Hume 7 Valse " Gay Paris" Burns 8 Selection 9 March " Occidental" Sousa ,10 Selection " Don Sebastian" Hume 11 Polka The Handy Man" Sheriff 12 March "Corporal Snook" Rimmer "God Save The King."

div.head: EARLESTOWN WAND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN WAND NEWTON.
HORSES ILL-TREATED AT NEWTON FAIR.

At the Newton Police Court, on Thursday, Henry Charlton, who had led a lame horse from Swinton, near Manchester, to Newton Horse Fair, on May 26th, was fined 20s. and costs.—Griffiths Baxter, the owner of a horse which had a sore back on the same occasion, was fined 10s. and costs.

div.head: BENEFIT CONCERT AT EARLE TOWN.
div.p: BENEFIT CONCERT AT EARLE TOWN.

On Thursday evening, in the Welsh Methodist Chapel, Earlestown' a concert for the benefit of Mr. Robert Jones, who has had to give up his work through illness, was given before a very large audience. A varied and enjoyable programme was submitted, consisting of a pianoforte solo by Miss Profit; songs by Miss Watkins, Mr. R. Robinson, Mr. E. Edwards; recitations by Mr. J. Williams; selection by the Y.M.C.A. choir, and phonograph selections.

div.head: MOTOR AND CART IN COLLISION AT NEWTON.
div.p: MOTOR AND CART IN COLLISION AT NEWTON.

A horse belonging to Mr. Samuel Winstanley, fruiterer, Winwick, was proceeding along Parkside-lane, Newton- le-Willows, on Saturday evening, when the approach of a motor proceeding from Bournemouth to Blackpool caused the animal to prance, with the result that the motor car collided with the vehicle. The cart shafts were broken off, Winstanley was thrown headlong into the road, and received lacerations about the head. The motor landed in a ditch, and it required two horses to replace it on the road. The motorist at once set out for Warrington, and obtained the services of a medical man to attend to Winstanley, who was taken home. The motorist escaped uninjured.

div.head: CIIARGE AG uNsT AGil/r:Ert. .
div.p: CIIARGE AG uNsT AGil/r:Ert. .

Herbert Huxley Duke, grocer, Earlestown, was charged at Newton Police Court, on Thursday with having used a piece of Raper under the goods pan of a pair of scales whilst weighing sugar. The prosecution stated that the paper was placed under the pan to make up for the paper in which the sugar was subsequently wrapped. The scales without the paper were nine drachms out of balance. In cross-examination Inspector Shepherd stated that the weighing of sugar was con- tinued openly in his presence. Defendant told him that the paper was worth more than the sugar. The defence was that it was a trade practice, and did not amount to fraud, and evidence to that effect was called the bench dismissing the case.
PUG MIST IC PARENTS AT E A ELESTO WN.

The magistrates at Newton-le-Willows Police Court had before them on Thursday Joseph Kelly, ex-militia man, and his wife Mary, residing at Athol-street, on a charge of illtreating their five children. The evidence of the prosecution was to the effect that both defend- ants were addicted to drink, the man would not work, and the children were shockingly neglected. It was stated that whilst under the influence of drink the woman attemptsd to drown herself on the 29th May. The male defendant was engaged in a couple of fights, in one of which he was 9tripped to the waist, and finished off with his hair, face, and clothing covered with blood. The woman also engaged in combat with another female, and because Mrs. Kelly did not get the better of her opponent her husband rushed at the vic- torious woman, struck at her with a hatchet, but hit a man. A witness to the fray rushed to the police station and reported that the woman had been killed. The police found the female defendant in a serious state of hysterics under the influence of drink, and the male defendant bearing evidence of Orions bruising.—The bench committed both defendants to gaol for two month's hard labour.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ST. HELENS GLASSWORKS STOPPAGE.

The Sutton Glassworks, St. Helens, are about to cease operations. On Wednesday detailed notices, following up the general notice given some time ago, were posted in the various departments. The works have been offered for sale asa going concern, but it is not known if there is any likelihood of them being taken up by any other firm or company.

div.head: HAYDOCK MAN'S HIDDEN TREASURE.
div.p: HAYDOCK MAN'S HIDDEN TREASURE.

An inquest was held at Haydock, on Wednesday after- noon, on the body of James Jones, agod 70, of 156,- Church-road, Ha.ydock, who was found dead in his house on Saturday morning last. The evidence showed that the deceased had lived by himself for 17 years. The only article of furniture in the house was an old sofa, which had been converted into it bed, but on deceased's son searching the contents of a box, he found an iron tube, containing 65 sovereigns. These the son took possession of, and then reported the matter to the police. Dr. Hayward, who had made a post-nwrtem, said the deeeased must have been dead several -days before he was found, and death wls due to natural causes. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical , evidence.

div.head: HAYDOCK COLLIER'S COMPENSATION
div.p: A HAYDOCK COLLIER'S COMPENSATION

His Honour Judge Collier was asked to arbitrate, at St. Helens County Court on Wednesday, on a claim under the Workmen's Compensatibn Act, in which Catherine Morris, of 46 Lyme-street, Haydock, claimed £225 compensation in respect of the death of her husband, Edward Morris, who was killed in one of the Haydock collieries on April 21st last by a stone falling from the roof and killing him on the spot. The claim was disputed on the question of jurisdiction, the widow having resided in Ireland until after the accident. Mr. H. L. Riley represented Mrs. Morris, and Mr. E. Pease the colliery company.—Mr.,Pease, at the outset sub- mitted that the proceedings were bad, and that the plaintiff resided out of the jurisdiction.—Mr. Riley said that the sum which he•claimed to be due was £199 lie. With regard to the question of dependency. it would probably be urged that the wife had a small agricultural holding in Ireland; but the woman would tell them that the holding was only'rented at .£4 15s. and produced nothing more than the rent per year.— The judge found that the woman was entirely dependent upon her husband, and awarded her £199 lie.

div.head: Baptist Church, Golborne-street.
div.p: Baptist Church, Golborne-street.

On Stmday' evening the pastorpreached on "Christian Socialism," this being the last of a series of addresses on " Christianity and Social Questions," and stated that though there might be false systems of socialism,. socialism itself should not therefore be condemned. Socialism had come to stay, and it was the duty of the Church to take up the subject. Sosialism required that a man who wished to work should be able to do so, that he should not be overworked, that he should be well housed, well fed and well clothed, and have his share in all the privileges of the community. The Church had so far ignored its claims and the only way to truly serve one's fellowmen was by first of all being conse- crated to Jesus Christ, for love to God resulted in love to one's neighbour.

The Salvation Army. Brigadier Holmes conducted special services at the Salvation Army Barracks in Academy-street during the week-end. Well-attended services were held on Saturday evening and on Sunday, morning and even- ing. On Sunday afternoon the Brigadier gave a lecture !entitled " A modern Eldorado," which at- tracted a good audience. Alderman Smethurst pre- sided, and referred to the good work done by the Salvation Army.

Id.,the property of I James Harrison.—Mr. Madden, who prosecuted in the case of housebreaking, said on April 17th Mrs. Harrison went out about eleven o'clock, and when she returned at 12.30 she found the house window had hem broken near the catch. The house had been ransacked, and Mrs. Harrison missed the articles mentioned. Prisoner pawned the shawl for is. 6d., but in the meantime Mrs. Harrison informed the police, who searched prisoner's house abd found the carpet bag., He could not account for it to Detective Foster, but pleaded guilty to taking the smaller things. Prisoner was on ticket-of-leave.—Mr. G. Formby prosecuted in the first charge. He said prisoner went into a hair- dresser's shop in Scotland road, Warrington, and ised such bad language that the hairdresser refused to shave him. Whilst he went for the police, prisoner decamped with a razor.—With regard to the bicycle Mr. Madden explained that prisoner took it from the yard of Mr. Johnson, babinetfmaker. He was seen to take it, and on being spoken to he grumbled and took it back. A detective subsequently found the dinner basket at pris- oner's house.—The Chairman said prisoner had a very bad record. He had been pursuing a career of crime since 1895, and in 1900 was sentenced to three years' penal servitude for larceny. After serving two years prisoner was allowed out on ticket-of•leave, but he would now have to go back to complete his term and do a further twelve months' hard labour.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

TF:NANTS AS3AULT THE LANDLADY AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Police Courton Friday before Mr.H. Roberts and other justices, Richard and Mrs. Hughes, 10, Back.Atherton-street, were summoned for assaulting Sarah Cliffe, 83, Manchester-road,fon May 25th. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant, but the defen- dants were not legally represented.—The facts of the ease as stated by the complainant were that defendants were the tenants of one of her houses and a distress war- rant was levied on them for arrears of rent. When Mrs. Cliffe went to collect the rents on the date in question she was unaware that the distress warrant had been levied. Both defendants called her badi names and the male defendant aimed :a blow at her which she avoided byl stepping back. The yard gate was then locked and Mrs. Hughes struck •complainant in the back and also seized her by the hair. A girl named Jane Campbell who had accompanied the complainant climbed over the rails and unfastened the gate and the complainant then left.—Defeniants denied the assault but the magistrate; ordered then to pay costs amounting tG 10s.

LIVELY SCENE IN LIVERPOOL-ROAD. There was a lively scene in Liverpool-road on Satur- day, the sequel being that John Jackson, a labourer residing in Beswick-street, appeared before the magis- trates at the Borough Police Court on Monday. He was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Liverpool-road at 11.5 on Saturday night, and assault- ing Police Constable Hewitt, Train Conductor Mellor, Elizabeth Green,Ann Jane Miller and Agnes Miller—P.C. Hewitt stated that he saw a crowd congregated in the vicinity of the Bowling Green Hotel, Liverpool-road and ascertained that it was caused by the prisoner,who was drunk and acting in a very disorderly manner. He took the man into custody, and prisoner then kickel him about the legs. They fell to the ground together, prisoner using the most filthy language. Conduc- tor Mellor came to witness's assistance and prisoner was taken to the Police Station. He kicked and struggled on the way—Ann Jane Miller, Glasshouse Row, gave evidence as to prisoner's" assaults on herself, Elizabeth Green, and Agnes Miller in Factory Lane. Prisoner was following Mrs. Greenand she told him to go away whereupon he struck her three blows about the body. Witness called the attention of a man to prisoner's conduct, and pris- .oner struck her on the arm Witness's mother then came on the scene and prisoner struck her and the baby she was carrying.—The Chief Constable said this was prisoner's 16th appearance. He had had three months •on two occasions'for neglect of children.—He was sent to gaol for three months. 1"'

THEY FROM A WARRINGTON WIRE WORKS. At the Warrington Police Court on Saturday, before Mr. Hayward (presiding) and other magistrates, Thomas Morris, Orchard-street, was charged with stealing' twenty-four pieces of soap value 25., from the works of Messrs. Rylands Bros., Church-street, and Bridget Harrop, Orchard-street, was charged with receiving fourteen pieces knowing them to have been stolen.— From the Chief Constable's statement it appeared that the male prisoner was a labourer at the works, and had been employed on the night turn from time to time. He had taken advantage of this by going round and appropriating soap which had been left about the pre- mises by workmen. The soap was specially prepared for use by wireworkers, and the firm had I.st a -great quantity of it by pilfering. Prisoner appeared to have taken the soap home and sold it. One Sunday morning about three weeks ago he was standing at the 400 r of his houseand called the prisoner Harrop to him. He told her that he was "dying for a drink" and she gave him 2.1 d. for fourteen pieces of the soap. Mrs. Harrop's husband worked at Messrs. Rylanils's and she must have known that prisoner had no means of obtain- ing soap of that description except by stealing it. In order that her husband should not know that she had obtained the soap she stored it at the Whouse of a neighbour named Elizabeth Tully for some time. Mrs. Haerop must have known perfectly well that she was receiving stolen goods. A number of women seemed to have handled the soap but there was no evidence that any of them except Mrs. Herron knew they were handling stolen property. —Evidence was-given by Mary Barton and Elizabeth Tully, the last named witness stating that Mrs. Harron had told her she was sorry she had had anything to do with the soap.—Superintendent Monaghan deposed to arresting the prisoners against whom there was nothing previonsiv.—Counzillor Hulse, secretary to Messrs. Rylands Bros., said the male prisoner had borne a very glod charactn. The firm had suffered considerably by pilfering and had brought the case forward because they wished an example to be made.—Morris was fined 20s. with the option of 1-1- days'imprisonment and Harrop was ordered to pay sc. or in default seven days' im- prisonment.

After he left the brandy was missed. The police were informed, and Sergeant Bourne visited the prisonbr's lodgings, where he found the empty bottle. Prisoner said he was drunk at the time and' did not know anything about it. Leigh now expressed his regret at having stolen the brandy. div.head: Minor Cases.
div.p: Minor Cases.
Warrington Borough Police Court.

PrateAy.—Before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, Messrs. Hepherd and Thornton. CASE DISMISSED.—The magistrates, after hearing evidence on both sides, decided to dismiss a case in which Thomas Morris, 17, Orchard-street, was sum- moned for assaulting Mary Barton, 8, Orchard-street. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A. WlFE:—George Pritchard, 4, Queen-street, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Esther Pritchard, on June lst.—Defendant did not appear.—Complainant alleged that her husband struck her in the face and on the top of the head when she returned home on Monday night. Since the alleged assault he had not been near thee, house.—The magis- trates granted a Warrant for the defendant's apprehen- sion.

SEPARATION ORDER GRATED.—Henry Britton, 68, Winwick-road, was summoned for persistent cruelty to his wife, Elizabeth A. Britton, but did not appear.— Complainant informed the Bench that defendant had frequently turned her out of the house and on one occa- sion he threatened to cut her throat. He had thrown the family Bible and several ornaments at her, until she was e.bsolutely afraid to go into the house when he was there.---The magistrates granted a separation order with 10s. per week alimony.
SATunDAY.—Before Messrs. J. W. Hayward (presiding)

and R. T. Fairclough, and hr. Fox. A DESERTER.—John Friar was charged with being a deserter from the sth Royal Trish Lancers stationed at Colchester.—The Chief Constable said prisoner surrendered himself to the police.—He was handed over to a military escort.

HUSBAND CHARGED WITH ASSAULT.—George Pritchard, Queen-street, was charged on a warrant with assaulting his wife Esther Pritchard on the Ist inst.— Complainant said prisoner callo. her foul names and struck her on the top of the head and in the face.— Prisoner said he had been doing work in the house for the complainant all day and in the evening she hit him in the face.—The case was dismissed.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, and Messrs. T. Birch%ll, J. W. Hayward, H. Thornton, and S. Wright. COMPLAINANT COULD NOT BE FOUND.—On the names of William Kenny and John Callaghan being called out the Chief Constable stated that it was a case in which a warrant had been taken out two years ago. It was a private case and now the man Callaghan, who had taken the warrant out, could no be found. lindor those circumstances Kenny was entitled to be discharged.— Kenny was then formally discharged.. STREET FOOTBALL.—Martin Burke, 8, Stanley-street; John Morgan, 7, Stanley-street; Martin Burns 4, Stanley-street; and John James Toughey, 7, Haks- place, were summoned for playing football in Barbauld- street, on May 26th.—Police Constable Clough said he had repeatedly warned the defendants about playing football previously, but on the day named they were kicking a bag, which had been rolled up, about the street. It as unsafe for anyone to walk down the street.—The Chief Constable said he had received com- plaints about such conduct. Mr. Potter, of the Royal Court Theatre, was constantly annoyed by that gang of boys.—The Chairman, in fining defendants ss. and costs each, said they (the Bench) were determined to put a stop to street football.

DISOR Dr:lL—Margaret Preston was fined ss. and costs for making loud and unseemly noises in Dolman's-lane on May 23rd.—P.S. Barnettand P.C. Stewart proved the case. Ellen Roberts, 18, Back Crossley-street, Mary Barton, 8, Orchard-street and Wm. Bates, 62, Allen- street, were fined ss. each for sirbilar offences.

O.RSCENT. LANGUAGE.—Mary Harris 15 Pierpoint- street, was fined ss. for making use of Harris, language in Pitt-street on May 23rd.—P.C. Reddington laid the information.—Mary Fisher, 11 Dial-court and Lawrence Speneer' Rose and Crown-street were mulcted in a like amount for similar offences.

HORSES ILLTREATED.—Anthony Manley, "Sister of Nazareth House," Ditton, was summoned for illtreating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state on May 20th. P.C. Cooper stated that he saw the defendant in Horsemarket-street in charge of a mare attached to a van. The animal was exceedingly- lame on the off-hind leg. He told the defendant lie could not travel it any further in that condition, and the mare was taken to the Patten Arms. Inspector Print, R.S.P.C.A., said he examined the animal, which was in very good condition hut was exceedingly lame on the hind leg from spavin. Veterinary Surgeon Dixon said the horse had the appear- ance of having chronic lameness. In reply to Mr. Connor, solicitor, who appeared for the defendant, Mr. Dixon admitted that the horse was in very good condition apart from the lameness. Mr- Connor said that the horse was used for carrying out a work of mercy and there was no deliberate intention to illuse it. A fine of 2s 6d, was imposed.—Samuel Platt, 6, Derby-street was summoned for working a horse while in an unfit state on May 19th, and George Buckley 64, Knutsford road, was summoned for causing it to be worked. Inspector Print said he saw the horse on Pig Hill, attached to a lorry laden with timber. Noticing thitt it was very lame he Stopped it. On examination he found it to be an aged animal, in poor condition, lame on both forelegs and suffering from ringhone and sidebone. Both hind feet were cankered,and the off hind limb was very lame. The shoe was broken and pressing into the foot. Platt told witness that Buckley had sent the horse out. Buckley denied that he had sent the horse out and Platt now stated that Buckley had not done so—As there was no evidence against Buckley the case against him was withdrawn, and Platt was fined lOs and cost.

TiiEsDAY.—Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair) and Hutchinson and Mr. J. R. Young. WIFE MAINTENANCE.—A man named Thomas Rooney was charged with arrears of maintenance due to his wife amounting to £3 4s. 6d. The magistrates ordered prisoner to pay the money or go to gaol for a month. • AN OBNOXIOUS LODGER.—John Heaton, of no settled abode, was charged with "sleeping out" at a lodging- house in Friars' Green.—Henry Kermode, manager of tip lodging house, said prisoner asked to be admitted to the house but as witness had had some trouble with the man previously he refused to allow him to enter.— Witness went to bed at 12-15, was aroused by the deputy mnnager and on going into the kitchen found prisoner lying across a form fast a.sleep. He did not know how prisoner got .there.—Prisoner, who is an old offender, was sent to riowol for 14 days.

div.head: Examiner, Friday, June 12, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, June 12, 1903.
- LOCAL WEDDING.

Stratton wis en fete on Thurslay last week when the marriage of Mr.Sarauel Davies,son of the late Mr. Peter Davies,of Warburton, and Miss Edith Mary Darbyshire, eldest daughter of Mr. Hugh Darbyshire, Shep- croft Far n, Appleton was solemnized at St. Matthew's Parish Church. The bride and bridegroom are well known and highly estee lied in the district and the wadding aroused widespread interest. The village , wore quite a festal garb, if igs and bunting being freely displayed. Prettily decorated arches spanned the road to the churl and the good wishes of the inhabitants found appropriate expression in mottoes such as "God bless the bride and bridegroom" and "Success to the brideand bridegroom." Prior to the ceremony the bells in the old! Church tower rang out a merry peal, and a large congregation- assembled in the Church. The service was fully choral, the choir being in attendance. The hymns "The voice that breathed o'er Eden" and "Oh Jesu I have momised" were sung. The Vicar of Stretton (the Hon. and Rev. C. F. Cross) officiated. The bride, who was given away by her father looked charming in a dress of ivory Indian silk over white glace silk trimmed with ecru lace and accordion pleated chiffon. She wore a veil and wreath of orange blossom and carried a lovely shower bouquet of orchids and lilies of the valley, the gift of the bridegroom. Shoals° wore a gold tiara set with pearls and turquoise, the present of the bridegroom. There were two brides- maids—Miss May Darbyshire (sister of the bride) and Miss Mabel Darbyshire (cousin of the bride), and they were becomingly attired in dresses of white silk over pink, trimmed with insertion and pink chiffon, with large picture hats to match. Their bouquets were com- posed of pink carnations and lilies of the valley, and they wore gold brooches set with diamonds awl pearls, the gift of the bridegroom. The duties of best man were discharged by Mr. John Hall (cousin of the bridegroom), and Mr. Percy Darbyshire (brother of the bride) acted as groomsman. Mr. J. Parkinson presided at the organ and played appropriate music and the wedding party left the church , to the strains of Mendelssohn's Wedding March." The Church bells again rung joyfully after the wedding a.ndalso welcomed the arrival of guests in the evening. The reception was held in a marquee which had been erectedat the house of the bride's father, and sixty gue3ts attended. In the evening dancing was indulged in, the music being supplied by Mr. Kendrick's band. I The catering was in the hands of the Winmarleigh Cafe I Company. The Church choir and ringers were enter- tained to supper at the "Cat and Lion" Inn and amid the good wishes of their friends the newly married couple made their departure for London at five o'clock en route for Brighton and the Isle of Wight where the honeymoon will be spent. No fewer than 136 presents were received, and they included a handsome clock from Mrs. Lyon, Appleton Hall. The bride's gift to the bridegroom was a pair of gold cuff-links.

div.head: NORTHROP'S LOOMS ON TRIAL. The Experience of a Lancaster
div.p: NORTHROP'S LOOMS ON TRIAL. The Experience of a Lancaster
Four-Loom Weaver.

The report of the Mosely Commission shows that Americans seem quicker than we are in adopting labour-saving machinery. In the textile factories of Lancashire the weavers have now the question before them "Will the Northrop loom supercede the old Lancashire loom ? Weavers should be thankful if it will stop "over-driving "and prevent "the weak from going to the wall." A strong and healthy woman can turn out more work from her four looms than a delicate girl, and it is therefore to the advantage of employers to 'have their hands in airobust state of health.

Amongst those who can speak from experience of such matters is Miss Belle Marshall, who resides with her widowed mother at 43, De Vitre-street, Lancaster. A representative of the "Lancaster Guardian" who called at the house of Mrs. Marshall the other day, was told that Miss Marshall was once in a very poor state or health. Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people hadput her right again. She is a four-loom weaver in a mill where Northrops are being introduced, and enjoys regular work and good health.

"But that has not always been the case," said Miss Marshall. "I suffered for several years from anmia, and was often at work when perhaps I should have been at home. But I did not believe in giving up till I was absolutely compelled. I took my food fairly well, but did not seem to get the strength from it that I ought. I was at last advised to try Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. I purchased Ri box, and I found that they did me a great deal of go6d. My food began to benefit me, and I felt my strength returning. I con- tinued to take the pills, and by the time I had finished the contents of eight boxes I felt so well that I did not think it necessary to take anymore,"
"And you have hail excellent Ilealth i3ince ?"

"Yes, feel as well as I look," Miss Marshall stated that she followed her employ- ment from 6 a.m. to 5.30 p.m., and was quite strong enough for the work, besides being a teacher in the Primitive Methodist Sunday School.

div.head: DRAYMAN KILLED. Shocking Accident at Stockton
div.p: A DRAYMAN KILLED. Shocking Accident at Stockton
Heath.

Charles Boswell, aged 47, a drayman in the employ of Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Co., Limited, residing at 10, Bluecoat-street, Warrington, met with a shocking death at Stockton Heath on Saturday evening. An in- quest was held on Monday morning before Mr. R. Dobson, coroner.

Alfred Arnold, 76, Victoria-terrace, Stockton Heath, drayman in the employ of Niessrs. Greeaall,Whitleyand Co., stated that on Saturday he and the deceased went in charge of drays to Northwich. Deceased was driving two horses, one in the shafts and the other a chain horse. They left Northwich at 3.45 and were returning to Wilderspool, deceased leading. Just before they reached Old London Bridge witness noticed that deceased's horses were trotting and when witness reached the top of the bridge he saw a large crowd a little way down the road. He went to the spot and found deceased lying dead in the roadway. John E. Sp msley, of Old 'Llndon-roaa, sthted that aboutB.ls on Saturday evening he was in the frclnt room of a friend's house in Old London-road when 'fie saw the deceased driving two galloping horses attached. to a dray. The chain on the off-side was unhooked and as the horses galloped it swung about. About twenty yards further on the drayi:struck the ) kerbstone on the right side of the road. Deceasedstuck to his horses but the dray again struck the kerbstone with such force that deceased was thrown off the vehicle on to the footpath, alighting on his head. Two barrels fell immediately after him but witness could not say whether they struck deceased or not. Witness went out and held deceased in a sitting position. A neigh- 'hour brought some port wine but deceased was unable to swallow it.

Acting-Sergeant Bowyersaid he went to the scene of the accidert, and on examining the deceased found he was dead. His skull was fractured, and a quantity of blood was oozing from the right ear. Theupper part of the right arm was fractured and there were severe bruises on the chest, abdomen and thighs. The injuries to the lower extremities were very severe, and might have been caused by empty barrels falling upon deceased.
A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. ............•10......,,,1.m..•

Newton Cases at Liverpool County Sessions.

At Liverpool County Sessions on Tutjday,.Richard Dobson (37), labourer, for having, at Newton, on the 2nd May, 'stolen a lady's shawl, the property of William Jones,- was sentenced ' to six months' imprisonment. —llr. Madden prosecuted.—George Thomas Dean (25), labourer, and James Donoghue (33), collier, were charged with stealing two men's shirts at Newton on the 27th April, the property of Hugh Ellis Pritchard. Dean was discharged, and Donoghue was sent to prison for a month.—Mr. Oulton prosecuted. Warrington P.S.A. - - - - -

A well-attended open meeting of this society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Sunday, when Mr. Thomas Duckworth presided. Miss Hewitt sang " Ora pro nobis " and "The chadren's home" in a. very pleasing manner, being accompanied on the piano by Mr. W. Looker. Mr. John Crumble- hulme (Bolton) addressed the meeting, the title of his address being" Victor or victim." A. collection was made on behalf of the P.S.A. funds.

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING 1 SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING 1 SOCIETY.
A Satisfactory State of Affairs.

The annual general meeting of the above-named society—the 33rd in its history—was held on Monday evening in Golborne-street schoolroom. Mr. J. W. Bouchier was voted to the chair on the proposition of Mr. Isherwood, seconded by Air. E. Wallington. Amongst those present were :—Messrs. James Harding (chairman of the society), E. Wallington, E. Penton, R. Isherwood, J. Baxter, E. T. Turley, J. Wilding, W. H. Wallington, J. Williamson, A. J. White, Haviour, Owen, J. Potter, Smithson, Greely, with Mr. Longland (solicitor) and Mr. P. Dalton, (secretary).

div.head: TILE ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: TILE ANNUAL REPORT.

The following report was submitted:—The managers have pleasure in laying the Thirty-third Annual State- ment of Accounts before the shareholders. During the year the sum of £1,612 18s. 10d. has been received as subscriptions; £2,506 9s. for rep lyments and. interest; and £lB 7s. 9d. entrance fees, fines, Stc., making the total receipts £4,167 15s. 7d.; the working expenses being £6B 16s. The withdrawals amount to £1,751 55.9 d. The sain of £2,875 has been advanced to members. There are 221 subscribers, holding 290 shares ; and 40 borrowers, holding 2001 shares; making 281 members, holding 4901 shares. The bonuses this year amount to £503 2s. 6d. on the amount lent, of which sum £92 is divided as profit, and £lll 2s. 6d. carried to the prospec- tive interest account. Under the Building Societies' Act, 1894, the accounts of all building societies are required to be made up in such a form, and to contain such particulars as the Chief Registrar of Friendly Societies may, with the approval of the Secretary of State, direct. The form of account which has been prescribed by the Chief Registrar requires that the balance of capital remaining due upon the mortgage securities should be stated separately from thearospective interest thereon; in other words, the balance of the £B2 10s. (the nett amount advanced per £100) remaining unpaid is to be distinguished from the balance of the £l7 10s. (the bones charge) also remain- ing unpaid. The accounts of the society for the past year have been made `up on this basis, and work out as follows: The total amount owing upon mortgages is £18,702 Is. 3d., of which only £9,410 17s. 4d. can be regarded as capital, the balance of £1,261 '3s. 11d. representing the proportionate amount of in- terest thereon, calculated for the number of years the several mortgages have still to run. The profits for the year, including £14,105. Bd. from last account, after deducting working expenses, amount to £377 Os. 4d., out of which the managers recommend a dividend of four per cent., which will take £360 4s. 7d,, leaving a balance of £l6 15s. 9d., which they direct to be carried forward to next year's account. The whole of the Managers retire. Messrs. Harding, Wall- ington, Isherwood, Bouchier, and Baxter are eligible, and offer themselves for re-election. We regret to say that owing to infirmities Mr. Fenton feels compelled to retire from the Management. Six additional Managers will be taken from the Register in rotation.
THE CHAIRMAN AND THE RECENT BUILDING SOCIETY SCARE.

The CHAIRMAN said they had a very satisfactory balance sheet to place before the shareholders. There was a considerable increase in the total amount received, notwithstanding all the controversy there had been in Warrington over building society matters. They had always maintained that their society was absolutely safe. (Hear, hear.) The safety of the society not only depended upon its officials but upon the managers and every shareholder. Proceeding to explain the methods in which they conducted their. business. Mr. Bouchier said they met every Monday night, and three managers received their money,and the Secretary entered it up into his book. The bank book was on the table, and every manager could see, and did see, that the previous week's receipts had been duly placed in the bank. It was all very well to say they had a good secretary and one they could trust, but the more they looked after people the better it was for the persons themselves and for the shareholders. (Hear, hear.) This society did that. Their two auditors had to do their work. At the end of the year the managers gave notice that the pass books were required for ,the purpose of audit, and they got a fair proportion of them, but he was sorry they did not get more. It was almost an impossible thing to get all the pass books, but all that were received were compared by the auditors with the ledger and with the balance book. For the future they were going to have the balance book on the table at every Monday night's meeting,and any member who deposited could compare his own book with the balance book. It would be more satisfactory to thesociety. if each member would make a point of doing that. It would then be impossible for anything; to be wrong, and they wanted the society to be abso- lutely safe for everybody, and to be quite above sus- picion. (Hear, hear.) When they had the building society scare ita, Warrington they quite expected a run on their society, but quite the contrary was the case. During the last two or three months they received more money than in the early part of the year. That showed the confidence the shareholders had in them, which they hoped would continue. They trusted the members would help the managers and secretary by doing all they could to prove for themselves that the figures of the society were absolutely correct. They would also assist the secretary and auditors very much by sending in their pass books at the end of the year. What helped very much the unsoundness of a society was having a lot of property in their hands, especially property out of town whidh they could not see for themselves. That, unfortunately, had been the case with more than one building soci.ty,and depression consequent upon loss of trade had been thecause of the difficulties in most cases In that respect their society was very safe. (Haar, hear). They were a workingmen's society and all the property was in the hands of the members themselves. (Hear, he tr.) Another good feature was the management. They had six managers whom they might regard as somewhat permanent, but they had to be elected every year. in addition six managers were elected by rotation from the books, so thit all the members sometime or other became managers. He thought that a very good feature. (Hear. hear.) THE BALANCE SHEET.
The SECILETNRY (Mr. Dalton) then read the. balance sheet which he was about to send to the Registrar of Friendly Societies.

The CfrAIRMAN called attention to several points in the balancesheet, and pointed out that the total income exceeded last year's sum by £320, which was very good considering the amount of trouble there had been in Warrington. The Witfulrawals were less by £l92' and the cost of management, although the society had done mere business, was also slightly less. Their prospective interest account, which they might regard as their reserve fund was £1,261 3s. 11d., equal to £l2 12s. 2d. per cent. (Hear, hear.) M. R. ISFIERWOOD moved and Mr. E. Fenton seconded the adbption of the balance sheet. THE VALUE OF THE SOCIETY. IMPORTANT STATEMENT.

Mr. GREALFW asked what was the value of the property mortgaged to the society. He thought that would show the members and the public that this society was absolutely secure. A lot had been said about building societies and they were getting a bad name. He was glad the Cintirraanhad taken the trouble to show the members that their money was safely in- vested. He had absolute confidence in the, concern.

The CR:URMAS said Mr. Grealey gave noticea the question and he was glad to be in a position to answer it as it was a most important onc.. The amount owing on mortgages was £10,702.1s 3d. The lowest valuation of the Surveyors was £19,391—a difference in favour of the society of £9,000. (Hear, hear.) The highest valuation was £490 more than that.
Mr. GII.FALEIr thought the statement should give confidence to the members.

Mr. WALLINGTON said as one of the managers elected in rotation last year he could bear testimony to the careful way in which the society was worked. The bank book had been on the table each Monday night and had been examined. With reference to the system he might say only one person handled the money and an- other entered it up in the pass books. This was done independent of the secretary and it was almost impos- sible for a mistake to occur.
The balance sheet was unanimously adopted. A dividend of four per cent was agreed to on the motion of Mr. Grertlev, seconded by Mr. Haviour. - APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS. THE RETIREMENT OF MR. FENTON.

Mr. JOSEPH POTTER proposed the re-election of Messrs. E. Wallington, J. Harding, R. Isherwood, J. W. Bouchier, and J. Baxter as managers. He thought they had cause to be satisfied with the way in which the society was conducted. He was sorry to say he was a big loser in another society. Mr. GREALEV seconded the proposition, which was agreed to. The CHAIRMA. said he was sorry to have to say that 'Mr. Fenton was about to retire from the Ipanagement. As long as he (the Chairman) had been a manager Mr. Fenton had always been at his post, and he did not know a single instance of his absence. Mr. Fenton felt it quite impossible for him to attend to his duties any longer And they were all exceedingly sorry to part with him. As proving bis interest in tha society and his thorough faith in it, he (the chairman) might say that when the scare was on end they were expecting a run on the society, Mr. Fenton came to the schoolroom prepared to make a very large advance to the society

to tide them over any run there might have been, with- out having to call upon the bank. (Applause.) Mr. E. ISHERWOOD proposed that Mr. W. H. Walling- ton be appointed manager in the place of Mr. Fenton. Mr. E. IVALLINGTON regietted Mr. Fenton's retire- ment, but seconded the nomination of Mr. W. H. Wallington, Who had shown great ability in the manage- ment of the business. He did not know anyone who took a greater interest in the society. The CHAIRMAN supported the motion and coirobor- ated Mr. E. Wallington's statement. Mr. GREALEY moved that Mr. Haviour be appointed. He had every confidence in Mr. Wallington, but he did not want the business to be in one family. (Laughter.) Mr. HAVIOUR declined the office, as he had not time to give to it. He was in favour of Mr. Wallington. The CHAIRMAN said he had a family connection with Mr. Wallington, but did not think that made the society any unsafer or interfered with the conducting of the business.

Mr. GREALEY said it caused talk when a concern was managed by practically one family and relations. Mr. W. H. WALLINGToN said he did not want the office if anyone else would accept it, but if elected, the society would have his best interests. He had opposed Mr. Bouchier, even though he was a sort of relation. Mr. W. H. Wallington was elected manager with one dissentient—Mr. Grealey. _ _ _

A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Fenton for his past services on the motion of the CmußmAN,seconded by Mr. ISHERWOOD, and supported by Mr. HIARDING. The last-named gentleman, who is Chairman of Directors, said it had been a pain to him to see the difficulty with which Mr. Fenton came to the meetings of the society during the past few months. Mr. FENTON said he was obliged for the confidence shown in him for the past 31 years. He was a member of the society when there was nothing for coming, and afterwards when they got 6d., so it was not the cash that induced him to continue in office. He had done his best, and he was pleased to say that was the best meeting he had seen since he had been a member. He had been connected with building societies for sixty years, and had never lost a penny. He contended money was more safely invested in that society than in banks, and he had known more banks than buildinr,societies to fail. He and his daughterhad £250 in thaesociety, and did not intend to take it out. He did not want them to think that becapse he was retiring he was withdrawing his interest in the society. Messrs. W. Bodle, jun., and Robert Lee were re- elected surveyors, and Messrs. A. W. Howard and G. Armstrong auditors. DIRECTOR'S ALLOWANCE.
On the motien of Mr. GREALEY, seconded by Mr. EVANS, it was decided to make the directors an allow- ance of is. each for every meeting attended during the year.

AN OBJECTION TO AN OPEN INSPECTION OF BOOKS. Mr. GREALEY objected to the ledger being open for in- spection at the Monday night's meeting, so that any- one could see how the other stood. Some precaution should be taken so that each member would only be able to see his own account.

The CHAIRMAN said the difficulty could be overcome by having a page for each shareholder, and the Secre- tary could turn to the page. Mr. GREALEY said that would be satisfactory. THE PRICE PAID FOR PROPERTY.

Mr. SMITHSON suggested that it would be to the in- terests of working men if, on the application form for prospective borrowing, the question asking for the amount of the purchase of the property could be de- leted. Men sometimes had a bargain, and it was not always advisable to give away the price. The society had their surveyors, and therefore the question was un- necessary. Mr. LONGLA.ND, solicitor to the society, said it was desirable the managers should know what was the price paid for the property, as they had to make advances on the property. Mr. E. WALLINGTON pointed out that the managers were placed in a much better position when con- sidering the question of advances, if they knew the purchase price of the property. The CHAIRMAN said it was very much to the interest, of the borrower himself that they should know thepur- chase price.

AIViEmsER said if the borrower had got a good bar- gain, the manager'who got to know of it. might be able to go and offer a little more and get the bargain. Mr. E. WALLINGTON : It would be a distinct breach of the trust.
After further discussion, the matter was allowed to drop.

'Votes of thanks were accorded to the sole surviving trustee, Mr., J. Hatton and to Mr. Longland. Mr. GREALEY said he believed Mr. Longland was a conscientious lawyer. (Laughter). Mr. LONGLAXD remarked that he was once told there was only one honest lawyer, and he had to be killed. (Laughter.) The meeting terminated with an acknowledgment of the Chairman's services.

div.head: CURIOUS OLD REMEDIES.
div.p: CURIOUS OLD REMEDIES.

Did you ever hear of "Syrup of Fox's lungs," or of "Essence of Toad's brains"? Both these substances used to be thought excellent cures for anlernia, debility and digestive troubles. At a recent inquest on a London child it was proved that the parents had given it a "remedy" which had been removed from the British Pharmaeopceia over thirteen years ago as being "pain- ful" and useless." It is surprising how many people instead of using medicines discovered by the light of recent science, apply to their ailments so-called remedies which make a boast that they have been in use fifty or sixty years. Writing recently on the subject, Dr. Andrew Wilson says:—

"I suppose the advance of knowledge, rapid and wide, causes many old remedies to pass away into the back. ground : supplanted, as they are, by the new." So it should be. 'rake the matter of a household remedy for instance. Most housewives now have on the shelf a box of Chas. Forde's bile beans, which are without doubt the finest family medicine which modern science has produced. Their action is totally different to that of the lold preparations. These , latter, in cases of indigestion and liver trouble, merely drive out of the system the collected impurities and leave the impaired organs just as bad as before. Bile beans, on the con trary, act directly upon the liver andstomach and tone these organs up to do their own work. Moreover, they are purely vegetable, they contain no aloes, bismuth, mercury, or any other mineral poison; they are not sugar coated, but enveloped in an impervious film ; and in a hundred and one ways are as superior to the old- fashioned liver medicines of the past as the railway train is to the stage coach. _

! Yet, strangely eriough, some housewives have not yet proved their value, but keep to some out-of-date inferior preparation. Even in medicine the old must give place Ito the new; and it is well it sliould be so. We no longer I bleed men for consumption or for fevers, and we should I no longer dose our livers and stomachs with pepsin' • bismuth, or other poison. If you have not yet tried bile beans, a 'free sample box will be forwarded you upon receipt of a penny stamp (to pay return postage) and this paragraph, with the name of this paper written across it. Post your application to the Bile Bean Com- pany's Leeds depot, and write your address clearly. Bile beans may be had for one and three half-pence or , two and nine per box from all chemists, but in purchas- ing see the name "Chas. Porde" on every box, arid don't accept any preparation with a name of similar sound, I nor any substitute whatever.

Presentation. There was an interesting ceremony at the Central I Station on Tuesday morning. Mr. Thomas Harding, who has been in the employ of the Jones Sewing Machine Co. Limited at Warrington for the past four or five years' left by the 8,50 train for Liverpool en. route for his home in Seattle, United States. During , his period of service with the Company Mr. Harding has • gained the esteem of his fellow employees who assem- . bled:in strong force at the station to give him a hearty "send off." As a tangible token of appreciation Mr. Harding was presented with a handsome gold mounted umbrella which had been subscribed for by the employ- ees. Mr. J. H. Hill,disfrict manager,made the presenta- tion,and in the course of a few well-chosen remarks,said , he wasvery sorry to part with Nfr.Harding,whorn he had ! always found to be a very upright and honourable man. Mr. Harding briefly replied, and said he ilhuld I always look back with pleasure upon his period of j service under Mr. Hill. He thanked the subscribers I very cordially- for their handsome gift. As the train Ileft tht station, Mr. Harding was vigorously cheered Cheshire Crops.—Favourable Outlook.

A Cheshire correspondent says :—Things have wonderfully improved since the warm weather arrived, and the outlook for the farmers at the presert time is a favourable one. Both meadow grass and clover have jumped up, and cereals have made good head- way and are looking well, though in many places oats have not done so well as usual. Travelling over a good part of the county on Saturday one noticed that; clover would soon be ready for cutting. Crops promise to be up to the averag3, but farmers ,in not a few of the districts fear that the yield will not be a heavy one if the dry weather continues. Some of the meadows were looking rather bare on Saturday and in need of a gentle shower or two. Harvesting opera- tions will commence in about a fortnight, that is so far as clover is concerned. Some of the farmers are even now preparing for this busy time. Potatoes are now showing themselves well, and heavy crops: are ant ici- pated, but the " earlies " will be somewhat later than usual. There will be very little Cheshire fruit this season. Everything in the fruit line seems to have been touched by he frost. In some of the dis- tricts which have long been noted for their fruit sup- plies there is really no promise of anything this time.

div.head: MR. R;PIERPOINT'S MARRIAGE.
div.p: MR. R;PIERPOINT'S MARRIAGE.
PRESENT FROM THE JUNIOR CONSERVATIVES.

Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M.P., was the recipient of a handsome present from the members of the Warrington Junior Conservative Association and Club on Saturday afternoon in recognition of his recent marriage. The gift took the form of a rose bowl of solid silver in wrought and hammered work, bearing the following inscription :—"Presented to Robert Pierpoiut, Esq., M.P., on the occasion of his marriage, December 17th, 1902, by the members of the Warrington Junior Con- servative Association and Club, June 6th, 1903." The presentation took place on the lawn at the Club in Orford-lane in the presence of a large assembly of ladies and gentlemen. Mr. E. Draper presided, and amongst those present were :—Mr. and Mrs. Robert Pierpoint, Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, the Mayor and Mayoress, Mr. Roger Parr, Mr. and Mrs. Vere B. Davies,the,Revs.E.C.E. Carleton and W. Braceca.mp, Mr. E. J. Hall,Aldermen Smethurst and Hutchinson,Council- lora Bennett, Forshaw, and Hulse, Mr. H. J. Westbrook, Mr. J. Fulton Smith, Mr. W. L. Williams, Mr. L. Voisey, Mr. J. H. Smethurst, Mr. S. Sutton, and Mr. Holbrook (Conservative agent). The CHAIRMAN said that in welcoming Mrs. Pier- point, he felt sure they would all agree that in her they would have an ally who would be a very great force in the politics of Warrington in the future. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Strong as their efforts had been in the past on behalf of Mr. Pierpoint, who had been triumphantly returned at the head of the poll on so many occasions he could assure Mrs. Pierpoint that the work in the future would be done with greater vigour, knowing that they would be fighting not only under the banner of Mr. Pierpoint, but also that of the lady who had become his wife. (Applause.) Mr. ROGER PARR, president of the club, in making the presentation, said the members were very pleased to have the opportunity of presenting him with that token of their appreciation of his long services to War- rington and the Conservative cause. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Parr) was happy to be the mouthpiece of the Junior Association and Club to assure Mr. Pierpoint of their continued support, and to emphasize their heart-- felt intention of doing their utmost to support the Government which they were pleased he so efficiently upheld. (Applause.) He congratulated Mrs. Pierpoint on behalf of the association and club on that very happy occasion, and wished her and Mr. Pierpoint long life and much happiness. (Applause.) In responding Mr. Pi ERPOINT said that Mrs. Pierpoint and himself would value the gift very much indeed. They would lay great store by it, not only because of its intrinsic value and because of its beauty, but also, and perhaps more especially, because they would take leave to regard it as a token of estimation for them- selves and, might he say on an occasion of that sort, as some degree of affection. (Hear, hear, and applause.) That day he had the much-coveted opportunity of pre- senting his wife to them, and he hoped that in view of the long friendship which had existed be- tween the members and himself they would be anxious to extend to her the friendship that they had so long given to him. (Applause.) Need he tell an audience which consisted of so many of his supporters that Mrs. Pierpoint was a staunch Nn- servative. (Applause). At a social gathering of that kind he would be committing an error if he made a political speech, so he would leave broad politics alone. There were a good many people full of prophetic warn- ings who were pregnant with their own news, who told ' them that there was going to be a general election very soon indeed. He was not a believer in those sombre prognostications; he rather regarded them as mere °biter dicta, as mere inventions of the veriest officeboys of the Opposition newspapers. (Laughter.) Although there might not be a general election close at hand— they all knew the old proverb which they almost got weary of repeating: Keep your arms bright, your , guns loaded," and so on—it was just as well to remem- ber that a general election would come, be it near or far, and it was well that they should be always pre- pared. (Hear, hear.) If their party would only work in Warrington he had no fear as to the result of the next general election. Warrington had been since the great Reform Bill almost absolutely Conservative in its politics, and he did not think they were going to change so very much now. (Applause). On the motion of Mr. J. L. WILLIAMS, seconded by Mr. WILLIAM JOLLEY, Mr. Draper wal\ cordially thanked for presiding.

• THE LATE MR. BEAMONT. An adjournment was then made to the reading room where the Mayoress unveiled a bust of the late Mr. William Beamont, presented to the club by the sons of the late Mr. Robert Davies.

Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who presided, said it was most appropriate that a memento of one of Warring- ton's oldestand most respected townsmen should find a place in such a club as that—(hear, hear)—and of all parts he thought they would agree with him that the place most fitted for it was the reading-room. (Ap- plause.) They had all known and heard of the great literary tastes of Mr. Beamont. Sir Gilb,rt also alluded to the loss, which was felt throughout the town, by the death of Mrs. Beamont, who supported all the charities, and was well known by nearly everybody in the town. (Applause.) The MAYORESS unveiled the bust, and said :--It gives me great pleasure to have performed this inter- esting ceremony, and I feel sure that the gift will be much appreciated by the members of the Junior Con- servative Club. (Applause.) Mr. PIERPOINT moved a vote of thanks to the Mayoress for unveiling the statue of their old friend. He knew Mr. Beamont ever since he (Mr. Pierpoint) was a little boy. He knew him to be a good man, a pleasant man, a learned man and a most interesting man. (Applause.) Mr. J. H, SMETHURST, in seconding said they had long hopes that the Parrs of Grappenhall might con- tinue to take an interest in the conservative party in the future as they had d one in the past. (Applause.) The MAYOR in reply said he could more than endorse all that had been said of the late Mr. Beamont. He was a kind friend and a good man and they all rejoiced to see his bust had found such a resting place in that club. (Applause.) Councillor BENNETT proposeda vote of thanks to Sir Gilbert Greenall for presiding, and said Sir Gilbert ' was a descendant and representative of one of the finest old Warrington worthies of whom they had any record, and his father's name would long be green in the town for the public services he had rendered. That his son should be associated with that meeting in doing honour to another Warrington worthy was ideally appropriate. Mr. Belmont was like the late Sir Gilbert—an ardent and life-long Conservative; but Sir Gilbert served them in the House of Commons, and Mr. Beamont in the Council Chamber. He would like to suggest that the son of Sir Gilbert should emulate both. (Applause.) He hoped he would die at a very ripe old age, having had the satisfaction of representing War- rington in the House of Commons and the local House of Commons which stood in that pretty garden off Sankey-street. It would be appropriate for Sir Gilbert to come among them just now, because they all knew the interest he took in agriculture. It looked as if they were on the threshold of a controversy largely affecting the agricultural interests and he thought that of all Men Sir Gilbert could be of service at the next general election. In reply Sir GILBERT said he was afraid he could not do all the things Councillor Bennett had mentioned but when the election time came they would all be there. (Laughter and applause.)
