div.head: CORRESPONDENCE.
div.p: CORRESPONDENCE.
Summer Languor.
To TILE EDITOR OF TILE WARRINGTON EXAMINER.

Sir,--In the warm summer weather, when appetite fails.and languor and indolence creep over us, there is nothing more likely to destroy health zuld render the body liable to the attacks of diseasethan the pernicious habit of taking into the system excessive food. Very great care, in fact, is needed to prevent this being done. One source for the demand for food is the continual loss of heat to which the body is exposed by contact with the air and other surrounding object's. In summer this loss is greatly reduced. People who will persist in devouring as much food as they do in the winter, clog the system, and food which has been utilised by the tissues for the production of energy is cast back into the blood in a state of partial 'decomposition, and cannot be got rid of. without over- heating the body.

We ai.e often lectured about the evil effects of an over-indulgence in tea or coffee, not to mention intoxi- cating liquors, until many people are bewildered what to turn to for a summer beverage, which shall be at once agreeable to the taste, and supply the desired nourishing and stimulating qualities. Public attention has been freely drawn to the merits of Dr. Tibbles' Vi- Cocoa, as supplying a long-felt want in this direction. It is not simply a cocoa. but a nreparation of two or three other ingredients, which give it great nutritive and invigorating qualities. It is, thererore, not merely a pleasant beverage, but a food and a tonic in the bar- gain. Its success has certainly been phenomenal, and that is perhaps the best warranty for the claim made on its behalf, that Vi-Cocoa as a summer beverage is unequalled. As the proprietors continuo their generous offer of a dainty sample tin to anyone who will take the trouble to write to GO, 61 and 62, Bunhill Row, London, E.C., there is no reason why it should not be given a fair trial.
The tired languid feeling referred to certainly dis- appears when Or. Tibble9' Vi-Cocoa is daily used. Yours truly, SPECIALIST.
London, N.W.

Police Court and Prison Gate Mission. The folk wing. are the principal items in the work of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Liverpool Diocesan C.E.T.S. for the past month. The number of Police and Petty Sessional Courts visited lw the members of the staff is now twenty-six. The magistrates asked for and obtained the help of the missionaries on behalf of 119 persons, and the court officials and the police had their assistance for 88 pers as. At the Mission Room near Walton Prison breakfast, advice, help, &c., were given to an aggregate of 726 persons. There are numerous other items in the work of the Mission.

&CR-RESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and seat in, if possible,not later than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly. advised to write briefly. A short letter has a much greater chance of insertion than along one. We cannot under ordinary ciir cumstances undertake return themannscripts which are not used.

div.head: Stockton Heath's Education Needs.
div.p: Stockton Heath's Education Needs.

--- Sir,—Will you kindly correct an amusing error which crept in my letter of .last week upon this subject.—The -word" idleness "was accidentally substituted for the word " illaess " in the sentence referring to the over- crowding at the school. The sentence shordd read ." This overcrowding is alleged byseveral parents from time to time, to be a source of inness to their children." Thanking you in anticipation I remain yours .faith- fully,
E. ENGLAND.

div.head: ACTIOb BY A WARRINGTON AUCTIONEER. A Money-Lending Transaction.
div.p: ACTIOb BY A WARRINGTON AUCTIONEER. A Money-Lending Transaction.

An action for money lent, which had been remitted from the High Court, came up at St. Helens County Court on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Collier and a jury, when John Mainwaring and Co., sued William Joseph Wood of Warrington, and James and Jane Sumner, of,Callons Farm. Haydock, for £64 18s. 3d. balance of account. Mr. A. Browne represented the plaintiff and Mr. Rigby Swift defended. The particulars showed that £l7O was lent on June 17, 1897. £59 .9s. 10d. 'had been charged for the money at the rate of 6 per cent., and £164 lie. had been repaid in interest and principal. Defendants had paid .£33 Jss. into court. Mr. Yfainwaring said he had carried on business as an a,nctionetr and valuer at Warrington for twenty-six years. He had lent money to Wood's mother and step- father, and when the young man took a farm at Watery- lane, Eocieston; he applied for a loan. Witness lent him £l5O, and took two promissory notes, one for £lOO and the other for £7O. He charged £2.0 bonus on the loan, and 6 per cent. interest on the whole. He read the notes over and explained themeto the three defend- ants and others present. Mr. Rigby Swift asked the court to revise the bargain under 'the new Act applying to moneylenders. He argued that the £lO bonus and G per cent. made it a "harsh and unconscionable" bargain. Wood and three other witnesses for the defence denied that the promissory notes were read, and said that they only borrowed .£l5O. Nothing was said about a bonus. The judge said it was a serious question for the jury to decide. The jury found that the.£33 15s the balance less the £2O. and on a different calculation of interest, was sufficient. The judge said that was judgmenefor the defendants. Mr. A. Browne applied for a new triaL His Honour said it would not be proper to grant it on the spur of the moment. He suggested that the appli- cation should be made within twelve days, and he would consider it. He granted the defendants costs both of that court and on the proceedings in the High Court.

div.head: .PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL. The Nightsoil Contract.
div.p: .PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL. The Nightsoil Contract.

Dr. Murray presided at a meeting of the Penketh Parish Council held in the Wealeyan School-room on Monday•evening. There were also ptesent :—Messrs. C. E. Parker, J. G. Withinshaw, J. Millington, J. S. Snoddy, E. W. Clarke, J. Midwood, E. Foster (clerk) andl. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances).

• THE GAS QUESTION. The Clerk reported that he had forwarded a petition to the Secretary of the Gas Department of the War- rington Corpvation complaining of the variations and irregularities in the pressure of the gas supplied to the village. He received a reply stating that the petition had been handed to Mr. Haddock, gas engineer, who would,co doubt give the subject prompt attention. Mr. Withinshaw said that on Friday he bad two in- candescent lights burning in his room but the pressure was GO poor that a table lamp was required. Other members complained of the quality of the gas and it was decided to forward another letter specifying the date. mentioned by Mr. Withiashavv._

- - THE SIGHTSOIL CONTRACT. At the4ast meeting of the Council it was decided that tenders for the carrying out of this contract should be advertised for, and also that the pails and ashpits be emptied up to 12 o'clock noon with an interval between 730 a.m. ,and 9 a.m. and that no .work be done in the main street from 9 to 12 o'clock. The Chairman said he had interviewed Mr. S. Sutton (assistant clerk to the Rural Council) and Mr. Kerfoot in regard to the contract, and as there seemed to be some difficulty in the way of carrying out the Council's suggestions he suggested that Mr. Kerfaot should attend the meeting. The present contract terminated on June 17th and the meeting of the District Council would not be held until that day.-so that something would have to be done in order that the work could be carried out until the new contractor was engaged. Mr. Midwood raised a point as to whether Mr. Kerfoot, who was not a member of the Council, had a right to attend. The Chairman said the Council asked him to attend to the matter and if the members thought he had erred it was for:them to say so. Mr. Millington: I think you have done perfectly right. Mr. Kerfoot suggested that two days should be set apart for the work, the ashpits to be emptied on Mon- day and the pails on Tuesday. Mr. Snoddy thought it would be objectiStable if the pails were being emptied during the whole of one day, and he suggested that two separate half-days should be allotted to the work. Mr. Midwood was of the opinion that their business at the last meeting was a farce. They were now upset- ting the arrangements then made. It was stated that approximately there were 106 ash- pits, 243 pails, and 200 as-htubs in the parish. After considerable discussion during which Mr. Midwood re-asserted that the ILIA -meeting was a farce, it was decided to ask the District Council to invite Mr. Pownall to carry out the work for another month after the expiration of the contract, and it was also recom- mended that the pails should be emptied before noon on Tuesday and Wednesday. Mr. Snoddy said he thought the Council noted with pleasure the determination of the Inspector of Nuisances and the District Connell to have the work done satis- factorily in future. (Hear, hear).

div.head: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. The Ttade of the Town.
div.p: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. The Ttade of the Town.

'The meeting of this body was held under the presi- dency of the Mayor, Alderman W. W.Gossage, on Tues- day afternoon. There Were several interesting items placed before the members, chief amongst these being thereduction of the price of gas all round. Alderman Timmis, the chairman of the Gas and Water Committee, briefly reviewed the work of that depart- ment for the last twelve months, showing the profits made, which resulted in the committee conceding the reduetion of a Id. in the price of gas. Councillor Allen asked the committee to consider seriosaly the question on the minutes dealing with Horse v. Motor Traction. Several of the members on the Horses, Carts, and Stabling Committee asked for the mater to be put back for further consideration, and this was agreed to. At the close of the proceedings, Councillor Peters moved his notice of motion advocating the formation of a committee to look after and consider the welfare of the trade of the town, and its adaptability to com- mercial pursuits. His address on the subject was warmly received, and his ideas were endorsed by almost the whole of the Council. Councillor Davies said *he agreed with the motion, but he would not like it to be spread broadcast that Widnes is in a decrepit state. Councillor Peters thought the motion a prudent one, And it was unanimously passed.

div.head: BUILDING SOCIETY SENSATION. TRIAL OF MR. PROUD. Found Guilty but Leniently Dealt With. THE SCENE IN COURT.
div.p: THE BUILDING SOCIETY SENSATION. TRIAL OF MR. PROUD. Found Guilty but Leniently Dealt With. THE SCENE IN COURT.

[BY OUR OWN REPORTER.] 'The County Sessions House at Islingtoz, Liverpool was on Tuesday the scene of a trial in which all War--' rington may be said to have been more or less interested. This was reflected in the Sessions House itself, for whereyer one turned, a familiar Warrington face met your gaze. The occasion, was the trial of Mr. Robert Proud on several charges of falsification of the books of the Warrington Permanent Benefit Building Society. There was also a charge of em- bezzlement but Mr. A. P. Thomas, who prosecuted, stated that it had been decided not to proceed with the charge of embezzlement. Some minor cases occupied the attention of the Court until 11.45 and it was not till then that Robert Proud was called upon to answer the 'charges against him. MR. PROUD IN THE DOCK. On his name being called, Mr. Proud entered the dock. It was somewhat pathetic to see a man in the evening of his days, who has h.therto possessed a character beyond reproach, standing in the dock to meet such a serious charge. His grey hairs and ,patriarchal beard ctzuld hardly fail to excite the • sympathy of those incrurt, and his leading counsel ' (Mr. Tobin K. C.) was wise enough to seeit. His de- fence was based almost entirely on sentimental grounds. Mr. Proud's previous excellent character, his advanced age, his bad health and lapse of memory. With these, he appealed for the sympathy of the jury ' and argued that the false entries were not false entries at all, but mistakes due to lapse of memory. The jury nevertheless found him guilty of the charges of falsification of the books. The sym- pathies of the Bench had evidently been excited on behalf of the prisoner who now stood up to receive sentence. Sir William !Forward (the Chairman) !animadverted on the seriousness of the charge, which ,he characterised as a cruel imposition on poor I people and then to the surprise of those in Court and ' to the joy of the prisoner's family, he was bound over 'under the First Offenders Act to come up for judg- ment when called upon. . During the hearing of the case Mr. Proud was I accommodated with a seat in the dock. Through the iron grating one caught a partial glimpse of the prisoner, who seemed the least concerned of anyone in Court. In fact, his counsel stated that be had been asleep during the hearing of the case. Be this as it may. there was no lack of emphasis in his plea of "not guilty" when the indictments were read over to him. Immediately behind the dock sat his wife and four children—Mrs. Bunch, Mr. Tom Proud, Mr. W. Proud, and Mr. F. Proud—all of whom followed the case with painful interest and rendered whatever service they could in the defence of the accused man. To them the sympathy of all was extended in their difficult and distressing position.

MR. THOMAS OPENS THE CASE. In a cold, clear style Mr. Thomas stated the case against the prisoner. For thirty years, he said, the prisoner was secretary of the Building Society, and in the course of that long service he acquired the com- plete confidence of the directors and managers. Mr. Thomas detailed how the Chairman's suspicions became aroused at the action of Mr. Proud in connec- tion with the preparation of the balance sheet, and how they led up t.) the appointment of the special auditors and the presentation of their report. In relat- ing the methods adopted by Mr. Proud in making false entries, Mr. Thomas gave five typical instances. (1) The first instance they would go into, he said, was the case of a man named John Erlam. It seemed that by the depositors' ledger there wasdue on July 18, 1899, £4OO to Erlam, who had deposited that sum with the society. Nothing had been re- paid to him, and he died on April 23, 1900. Mr. Swain was appointed his executor, and on July 30th, 1901, there appeared in the society's book an entry by the prisoner of £4OO debited to Erlam's account as having been transferred to the journal. ' There was in fact no transfer, and the ,executors did not receive any portion of the £4OO. The prisoner, by that entry, apparently closed Erlam's account, and had £4OO to deal with. He kept the executor quiet, and he did not know anything of the entry. The executor received dividends for 1900 and 1901, so that his suspicions were not aroused. On January 29, 1902, prisoner opened an account in the name of the executor Swain and credited two sums of .£lO each to him, so by that means he repaid Swain £2O out of £4OO, leaving a balance of £3BO. (2) The next fictitiousadvance was concerned with a Mrs. Sarah A. Travis. She owed the society 400 on June 31, 1900, and on September 26 of the same year she repaid t 100, and got credit for it. That reduced the sum she owed to £3OO. In the ledger and in the cash book there Was an entry of £lOO made by the prisoner as being re-advanced to Mrs. Travis, thus making once more her debit £4OO. In the cash book that entry was put under date April 24, 1901. Mrs. Travis never received £lOO. It was a fictitious entry which enabled the prisoner to deal with that sum. (3) On December 18th, 1901, a Mr. Silcock who owed money on mortgage to the society, paid Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., solicitors to the society, the sum of £142 9s. Bd. and Messrs. Robert Davies paid it into the bank the credit of the society. It was prisoner's duty to enter it in the cash book on the debit side, and make a. corresponding credit so as to balance the trans- action. On one side prisoner entered the £142 9s. Bd. In two sums of £92 9s. 8d and £5O, and on the other side he only made an entry of £92 9s. Bd. (4) On January 28, £53155. was paid in cash to the directors, and a cheque was drawn on March 30, which was also entered whereas there was only one payment. (5). The last entry he would refer to was a transaction with the Widnes Corporation for street-1 making, to the extent of £152 7s. 4d. It was entered I as having been paid on January 28th whereas it was not paid until April Ist. Whether there was a payment at some other date which covered the amount was immaterial. It was sufficient he con- tinued, if the jury were satisfied there was a false entry at the time. It was somewhat complicated, to follow the transactions, hut the question the jury had to determine was whether the false entries were made for the purpose of misrepresenting the transactions for the advantage of the prisoner. THE LATE CHAIRMAN IN THE WITNESS BOX. Mr. Kenworthy, the late chairman of the society,was the first witness called. He identified the entry •of £440 in the bank pass blok as being in the hand- writing of Mr. Proud. He also identified the hand- writing in the books. Afterwards he related the cir- cumstances with reference to the balance sheet. He ' noticed that although the bank balance to the Society's credit the year before had been £52, at the end of 1902 there was a debit balance of £448. Asked to explain, Mr. Proud said it would be "all right." Subsequently the prisoner prepared a draft balance sheet, in which it appeared that the debit balance had been changed into a credit balance by a paym nt of £440 into the bank.

div.head: Examiner, Friday June 12, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday June 12, 1903.
observed that the witness did not appear to know much about books. THE ABSENCE OF THE AUDITORS.

Mr. Tobin added that he was in the difficulty of not having the auditors, Messrs Bolton and Dick, in the witness box to cross-examine them. The prosecution would not put them into the box. If they did he would not ask the witness another question. The auditors who made the special report, and who never went through the books with the prisoner were going to be called. He wanted to know the state of the pris- oner's mind and he could only get that from the auditors who worked with him or the President. There had been mistakes and he would endeavour to show there had been no intent to defraud.

Mr. Thomas remarked that if the auditors could speak in the prisoner's favour, they should be called by the defence. They would probably have to answer a good many difficult questions. The Chairman : It is quite evident theseauditers have not done their duty. Mr. Thomas (to witness) : You trusted, the auditors entirely ?—Yes, at the time. If they didn't find out, you couldn't find out ?—No. EVIDENCE OF THE SPECIAL AUDITORS.

Mr. Edwin Bradshaw, chartered accountant, and Mr. W. H. Woodcock repeated their evidence as to the re- sult of the special investigation. Asked by Mr. Tobin whether a child could not have detected the errors as they were so simple, Mr Bradshaw said no doubt some of the false entries were very simple, but all were not so. He declined to say anything as to the conduct of the auditors of the society. Despite the involved character of the evidence, Mr. Brad.shaw was paid a compliment by the foreman of the jury who said the witness was very clear on the points. Mr. Woodcock was asked as to the prisoner's state- ment to him on May 11th with reference to the pay- ment of £152 7s. 4d. to the Widnes Corporation. His remembrance was that Mr. Proud said he had not paid it. As a matter of fact he had, but not on the date entered in the books.

A number of other witnesses were called for the pro- secution, including Isaac William Turton, cashier at Parr's Bank, Warrington; Thomas Welsby, of Messrs. Robert Daviesand Company; Sarah Ann Travis, Central Promenade, Douglas, 1.0. AL, Newton Swain, grocer, 62, Liverpool-road, Mr. John Erlam's executor.

Society. It appears you held thisposition of great confidence and trust for a period of many years, and the evidence given is that you have been deliberately frauding this society, and you have been hiding up your frauds by false entries. The charge is a very serious one,a very cruel one because the society is composed of poor people who place their savings in the society, and by your actions they have been defrauded of a considerable part of their savings. We are deeply pained that a man of your position and honourable career should stand in the dock on such a charge. We have taken into consideration a long life of seventy years, daring the whole of which you have conducted yourself with great respectability, and also the fact, from the evidence, that you are in a bad state of health. We are going to strain an Act of Parliament which enables us to deal with you under what is called the First Offenders Act. Therefore you will have to come up for punishment when called for.—The Chairman asked the prisoner whether he was a householder, to which he replied in the affirmative. Mr. Tobin said he was instructed that the prisoner was not a householder, and ha would ask that the two sons be bound over as sureties.

Mr. Tom and Mr. William Proud then entered the witness box and were bound over. • Addressing them, the Chairman said the Bench felt that they (the sons) ought to look after the prisoner and take care that he did not go into any position again.
-Mr. Proud then left the dock and was congratulated by his friends on his happy release. A COLNE BUILDING SOCIETY SUSPENDS PAYMENT.

On Monday depositors in the Colue Permanent Build- ing Society received an intim ttion from the society's solicitors that discrepancies have been discovered in some shareholders' pass books calling for investigation, and that the directors have decided not to pay out money under withdrawal notices until such time as theauditors have completed their investigation and report thereon. Depositors are invited to regard the situation with calmness, as the reserve funds are believed to be largely in excess of discrepancies.

div.head: DEFENCE.
div.p: THE DEFENCE.

The first witness called for the defence was Mrs Proud, wife of the accused, who told the story of the prisoner's family life and of his lapse of memoryin re- cent years. She was married to him, she said, 40 years ago. Hehadonlybeen in two situations, first in the goods department of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, and afterwards as sub-manager for Crosfields, of Warrington. He was pensioned off by the latter firm. There had never been any charge against him. He was not extravagant in his mode of living, and did not spend money in drink or bett- ing or in entertaining, but lived a quiet life. As far as she could see, he was not spendinga penny more than he was getting from his work. She knew he had never had the money. It had never gone in or out of the house so fares she could tell. The children kept themselves before they were married, and cost him nothing except for education a good many years ago. Her husband had been losing his memory during the past few years. His office was next to the dining-room, and witness had often sat near the office doing her work. Shehad frequently seen two or threeneedy people oome and ask Mr. Proud to let them have some money. Witness had asked him whether hehad entered the money because she felt he had not done so,and on his returning to theocfice he had found that he had not entered the money. On many occasions she had reminded him about it. Sleeping and dizziness . had frequently come upon him during the last three or four years. Sometimes he fell asleep before finishing his meals. On one occasion she wanted to go out shopping and she asked her husband not to go to sleep while she was away. He replied, "No, I have too much work to do." Witness went upstairs when she heard a horrible noise. On looking down she saw her husband leaning over his books snoring and water was running from his mouth. He was in a kind of a fit. Since then he had been very strange in his manner about the house. One night after ten o'clock she went to bed and asked her husband to put the light out in the dining-room. He followed her up- stairs and when he got in the bedroom he said to her "Is Emma upstairs ?" (meaning witness.) She said "Robert, you know me, don't you ?" and he answered "I want to !mow where Emma is."
As a final question, Mr. Tobin asked: As far as you know has ever one penny piece gone dishonestly in your family? to which the witness replied "Certainly not."

THE SON'S EVIDENCE. Thomas Proud, the eldest son, gave evidence as to the ill-healfh which had been creeping over his father. He had notioed a great change, and he was of opinion that paralysis was coming over his father.—The Chair- man here interposed, with a question as to whether he I had ever notified the Society of his father's breakdown and witness replied in the negative. —The Foreman of the Jury said they would like some evidence as to whether Messrs. Crosfleld's pen- sioned the prisoner off owing to the state of his mind. Mr. Tobin replied that those were his instructions and he endeavoured to lead Mrs. Proud on to say so but failed. The Chairman then made a suggestion that the evidence which had been offered had little to do with the case. Mr. Tobin, with an impressiveness which one could admire, contended that the evidence offered was very important and had a great bearing on the case. Dr. Joseph then entered the box and said the prisoner was suffering from senile decay and in a condition which might result in death at any moment. MR. TOBIN ADDRESSES THE JURY. Mr. Tobin's address to the jury was an eloquent one and he may be said to have made the best of a we ik case. He appealed to the sympathies of the jury by referring to the prisoner's honourable career and his loss of momory. Dealing with the false entries, he said, "If a man over and over again forgot to enter payments he had made to needy people, or payments on account, or anything of that kind then, of course, in making up the books he would be tempted to put down inaccurate figures, not to cover up theft, but to cover up the consequences of his own loss of memory. That was not fraud." With great discrimination Mr. Tobin referred to a selected few of the charges which had been brought forward and tried to show that they were mere inaccuracies in book-keeping and that the money, in fact, had been paid. He wound up by a pathetic appeal to the jury " not to stamp an old man of seventy, who had lived a highly respectable life, as a criminal. ' MR. THOMAS SPEAKS IN REPLY. Mr. Thomas spoke briefly but to the point. He re- ferred to the painful duty they were called upon to perform. They all sympathized, he said, with the efforts that the prisoner's counsel had made to put the position of the prisoner in the most favourable light, but it was the duty of the prosecution to recall the real facts of the case. The false entries, he pointed out went back to 1893—at a time when Mr. John Crosfleld was a trustee of the society and obviously that gentle- man did not think Mr. Proud unlit to remain in his position of secretary of the society. If the jury had any doubt as to the unfitness of the prisoner for book- keeping he asked them to examine the books for them- selves. He proceeded to deal with some of the charges which Mr. Tobin had adroitly left untouched. He made a great point of the case of Mrs. Travis who had been debited with a re-advance of £lOO which she had never received. The altering of the bank pass book to make it tally with the balance sheet was not the mistake of a man, he said, who did not know what he was about. With reference to the treat- ment of the cheque from Messrs Robert Davies and Company, he contended that no one could suggest that it was a mere mistake. In a final word he said the prisoner had not given any. explanations. SUM4IING UP AND VERDICT. Sir William Forwood summed up the case to the jury with judicial skill. It was painful, he said, that a man at the close of a long and honourable career should stand before the Court on a charge of that kind. At the same time they were bound to do their duty . _ _ _ _ _ .

div.head: AN INJURED FINGER CAUSES DEATH. The Widow of a Wiredrawer Receives
div.p: AN INJURED FINGER CAUSES DEATH. The Widow of a Wiredrawer Receives
L3OO.

His Honour, Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C. was en- gaged for several hours on Thursday at the Warrington County Court in hearing a claim under the workmen's Compensation Act brought on behalf of the widow of the late Charles Thomas, a wiredrawer, of 106 Bostock- street, Warrington, and her daughter, who was a partial dependant, against the Whitecross Company, Limited. The applicant was represented by Mr. Wingate Saul (instructed by Messrs. Corbett of Manchester), and the respondents were represented by Mr. Adshead Elliott (instructed by Mr. Edwin Pears°, of Liverpool). Mr. Saul, in stating the plaintiff's case, pointed out that the claim was made by the widow as a dependant, and by the daughter,Ellen Agnes,as a partial dependant. The deceased, Charles Thomas, was 67 years of age, and was employed by the Whitecross Company, Ltd., in Warrington, and his employment was that of a wire- drawer. On the 4th of December last year, whilst in the employ of the Company, his hand was caught by some slack wire, which injured the third finger of his left hand. Shortly afterwards he went to the Infirmary and he was treated as an out-patient until the 25th December. He then went in as an in-patient, and it was found necessary to amputate the third finger of the left hand. This was done, and he remained there until the 6th January, when he returned home and died oil the 19th of January, of pleurisy brought on by his low condition of health resulting from the injury. Dr. Braid P had been the medical attendant of the family for ten years and he attended the deceased after he returned from the Infirmary. On the 6th January he examined him at home and found the pleurisy established in the patient's side. Prior to the accident the deceased was a healthy and strong man and the doctor always found that "a bottle or two" put him right. As a result of a post- mortem examination Dr. Bride would be able to state that it was owing to the low condition of health, re- sulting from the injury that set up the pleurisy. Mrs. Thomas, the widow, gave evidence, and stated that she was married on the 3rd November, 1856. There ' were 12 children seven of whom were married and four able to support themselves. The only one dependent of the deceased was a daughter, Ellen Agnes. Dr. Braide was then called and gave evidence of his attendance on the deceased after his removal home from the infirmary. The injury brought on the low state of health which induced pleurisy to be set up. Cross-examined: The man was not suffering from chronic bronchitis. When he examined the patient in the Infirmary on the sth he wasunder the impression that the deceased was suffering from pleurisy. He agreed that it was inadvisable to remove a patient suffering from pleurisy as was done in this case. He did not suggest to the Infirmary authorities that the man ought not to be removed, but Dr. Mort was pre- sent when he advised the deceased not to leave the institution. Pleurisy was brought on by a chill. Re-examined: The deceased's removal did not accelerate death.

William Charnock, manager for the respondent firm, said he had known deceased about twelve years. For the past five years he was under witness's supervision and during the last two years had made considerable complaints that his work was rather irksome to him. He asked for a lighter job and had he lived witness would have given him one. During the past twelve or eighteen months witness had noticed a considerable change in deceased's appearance. He appeared to be sinking and during the past year he had looked eight or nine years older. He would often come to witness physically exhausted and obtain a half-holiday. By Mr. Saul; He was not surprised that a man of deceased's age should be exhausted after lifting heavy weights. Deceased's average weekly earnings during the last three years were about 425. Bd. Dr. Mort, senior house surgeon at the Infirmary, said he examined deceased before amputating the finger. He formed the opinion that deceased was prematurely senile. His arteries were degenerated and the heart was slightly dilated. These symptoms could not have come on since the date of the accident. There was nothing actually wrong with the lungs but deceased had chronic bronchitis. The whole circulatory system was much degenerated. He thought deceased had pleurisy on January 4th. Previous to the operation deceased wife told witness that deceased had a very weak heart and was subject to fainting fits. By Mr. Saul; He didnot think deceased would have gone on lifting heavy weights if his heart was in a very bad condition. Professor F. F. Paul, a member at the Royal College of Surgeons, said that judging from Dr. Braide's notes of the post mortcm and the evidence which had been given that day he saw no evidence that the pleurisy was due to the accident. He had no doubt that pleurisy might have contributed to death but if it ha,cl been the actual cause death would have been more of an asphyxia character. He was of the opinion that the weak con- dition of the heart brought about pleurisy. Dr, Thomas Harris said Dr. Braide's notes were not consistent with a death from ashyxia. He could not see any connection between the accident and the pleurisy. Mr. Elliott contended that the pleurisy had not been brought about by the accident. His Honourheld that death was brought about by the aecident and awarded the widow £3OO and costs, the daughterhaving withdrawn her claim.

IMPUDENT MARKET ROBBERIES.

Two impudent market robberies were investigated by the magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday when Laura Trott and Ellen Clutterbuck, married sisters residing at 21, Catherine-street were charged with stealing a plush handbag, of the value of is., from the stall of Israel Ginsberg, in the Market- place, on Wednesday afternoon and also with stealing two pieces of silk, a piece of ribbon and a oollarette, valued at 2s. lid. from the stall of Emily Crossley.— The Chief Constable said the robberies to which the prisoner's had pleaded guilty seemed to be a never- ending class of offence. Between three and four o'clock on Wednesday afternoon the women were observed going from stall to stall. P.C. Burton and a gentleman named James Monks watched them. The modusoperandi adopted was for one prisoner to look at an article and put it down on the edge of the stall and the other prisoner would come along, gather it in and conceal it about her person. This method was employed in the two ofISEIS now brought forward. One of the women was quite a capitalist having no less a sum than .£7 or £8 in her Possession. Stall-holders had assured him that it was only one of every five or six cases of this description that was brought before the Court as they did not care Lo lose time in prosecuting.—Prisoners were sentenced to a month's hard labour.

div.head: GREAT FIRE AT WARRINGTON. MESSRS. FLEMING'S TANNERY GUTTED.
div.p: GREAT FIRE AT WARRINGTON. MESSRS. FLEMING'S TANNERY GUTTED.
Three Fire Brigades at Work. HOUSES IN -DANGER.

Thousands of Warrington people left their homes late on Monday night to witness one of the most disastrous fires which has occurred in the town for many years. The clanging of the fire bell at ten minutes past ten appr sed many of the outbreak, and later on the residents in the Bank Quay neighbour- hood were startled to hear the prolonged sounding of the hooter at Messrs. Crosfield's works. Soon ex- citement reigned supreme in the streets. "Where is the fire ? " was the question on the lips of almost every person one chanced to meet. At length the news gained currency that the scene of the conflagration was the large tannery of Messrs. J. H. Fleming and Co., Ltd., Fennel-street, and thither thousands directed their steps. A. brilliant red glare in the sky convinced the inhabitants that the fire must be one of tremendous magnitude, and their con- viction was, unfortunately, only too fully borne out. The Alarm.

Curiously enough, Mr. Frank Turner, the deputy superintendent of the Fire Brigade, was in the vicinity of the tannery when the alarm was given. It appears that Mr. Edward Smith, hairdresser, Fennel-street, saw flames issuing from the boiler • sheds, and the discovery was soon noised, abroad. Deputy Superintendent Turner assisted some employees of the firm to get their fire apparatus at work, but the men were entirely unable to cope With the flames. The fire brigade was promptly on the scene in full strength, Superintendent Turner as usual directing operati ms. The steam engines " Major" and" Cap- tain" were brought into requisition, a fairly good supply of water being obtainable.

div.head: Four Wines at Work.
div.p: Four Wines at Work.

Superintendent Turner at once saw that a heavy task confronted the firemen, and lost no time in telephoning for the Wilderspool and Messrs. Crosfield's brigades. These willing helpers soon arrived with their steam engines, the Wilderspool brigade being in charge of Engineer Craughton, whilst Superintendent Gallon directed Messrs. Crosfield's contingent. The members of the latter brigade had to drag their engine to the scene of the fire. We believe this is the first occasion on which four fire engines have been seen at work in Warrington at one time,and the only drawback was that with such a great demand for water, the quantity to be pumped by each engine was somewhat limited.

How the Flames Spread. The flames spread with marvellous rapidity and in an extraordinarily short space of time the warehouse was ablaze from end to end. The contents of this large six storey building were of a highly inflam nable HAture, and included thousands of finished hides. There was also a stock of oil and when this was reached the flames shot upwards with increased fury. At the out- set efforts were made to rescue the books and papers from the office, Mr. E. Lunt (secretary of the Company) and many willing workers assisting. Some of the books Sr.c.,were saved but others had to be left as the if was fast nearing the office and it was impossible for anyone to re nain there. A strong wind fanned the flames and when the fire was at its height the spectacle was appalling yet brilliant and must have made a lasting impression upon the minds of all who witnessed it. A vast crowd assembled and every coign of vantage was seized upon many people watching the conflagration from the house-tops. A large staff of police was in attendance under the personal superintendence of the Chief Constable and their efforts to keep the crowd at a safe distance from the burning structure were ably seconded by a detachment of soldiers from Orford Barracks under the command of Captain Goren. Alderman Smethurst, chairman of the Fire Engine Committee, was present and rendered assistance.

div.head: Houses in Danger.
div.p: Houses in Danger.

The tannery was surrounded by houses on three sides and the firemen had soon to direct thair attention to this property. The back portion of some cottages was actually alight and as may be readily imagined the occupiers were panic-stricken. Furniture and house- hold goods were removed with all haste into the streets and many goods remained out- side throughout the night. The firemen worked with a will and happily the wind veered round somewhat, thus diminishing the danger to the dwellings. The damage done to the houses was comparatively slight, but naturally the residents, filled with fear lest some calamity might befall them, had little rest during the night.

div.head: Tannery Gutted.
div.p: The Tannery Gutted.

Meanwhile the fire at the tannery continued with un- abated ferocity and it was seen that the building was doomed. At about 11.30 the roof fell in with a great crash, and gradually the entire structure was destroyed. As each part collapsed myriads of sparks filled the air and the high wind carried the embers a great distance, some being blown as far as Bold-street. Spectators were frequently in danger of having their clothing ignited, but no burning accidents have been reported. Some of the upper rooms in the warehouse contained machinery which crashed through the floors, a roller on the second storey weighing over two tons.

div.head: Narrow Escape and an Accident.
div.p: A Narrow Escape and an Accident.

Several members of the Warrington and Wilderspool brigades had a narrow escape. They were busily engaged in a passage adjoining the mill yard when the gable end of the warehouse crashed down. The men stepped aside just in time to avoid the falling mass of debris or the consequences would have been serious. Fireman Warburton, of Messrs. Crosfleld's brigade, was less fortunate. He was enga ed on the roof of an outbuilding when he slipped and fell to the ground, injuring his hip. He was taken to the Infirm- ary but after being attended to was allowed to go home.

Mr. Lee's Workshop Destroyed. Despite all efforts the workshop of Mr. Robert Lee, joiner, adjoining the tannery, fen an easy prey to the flames, and the stock of finished goods and seasoned timber was destroyed. Mr. Lee estimates his loss at between £201) and £3OO, but it is covered by insurance. Great praise is due to the members of each Fire Brigade who worked most harmoniously together. It was not until three o'clock on Tuesday morning that the fire was got under control and the Wilderspool and Messrs. Crosfield's brigades were dismissed. The Warrington brigade was engaged in playing on the smouldering ruins daring the whole of the morning and several of the bare walls had to be pulled down. When the flames had been extinguished the tannery presented a scene of devastation, the only structures which had been saved being the sheds in the yard which contain • the tanning pits.

div.head: Damage.
div.p: The Damage.

The damage amounts to at least £20,000, but it is covered by insurance. At about four o'clock in the morning another small outbreak occurred at a ware- house in Carlisle-street, some bails of bagging being ignited by sparks which had been blown from the tannery. -Firemen and police were at once dis- patched to the scene, and the flames were extinguished in a short time.
The services of the police and military detachment were invaluable, the great crowd being kept admirably under control.

div.head: ECHOES OF THE FIRE. Thieves Seize their Opportunity.
div.p: ECHOES OF THE FIRE. Thieves Seize their Opportunity.
Smart Penalties.

During the progress of the fire opportunity was taken to perpetrate two mean thefts, hut fortunately the offenders were discovered and brought to account be- fore Aldermen Sutton and Hutchinson at the County Borough Police Court on Wednesday morning. In the first case James Quigley, James-street, a well- known character was charged with stealing a silver lever watch, of the value of £2, from the dwelling- house of John Wright, 21, Fennel-street. He pleaded not guilty. The Chief Constable said this case was an echo of the great fire, and their worships knew from personal ob- servation and fro u the papers, that the fire threatened the adjoining cottages very considerably. Not only were they threatened on several occasions, but those immediately surrounding caught fire. Mr. Wright who was a fireman at Messrs. Walker's brewery lived in one of the houses, and at the time of the outbreak his watch was hung up in the bedroom. When danger threatened, willing hands helped to remove the furniture, (Ice., from the house. As usual there was a blaok sheep somewhere, and the magistrates now had hi ii before them in the person of the notorious Quigley. He (the Chief Constable) saw Quigley at the fire and, knowing him, placed n plain clothes officer to watch him. Prisoner avail.dhimself of the opportunity of entering the house and, going upstairs, took the watch, violently removing it from the chain to which it was.attachod. Mr. Wright missed his watch and made inquiries about it. The prisoner was about the streets until two o'clock, but never went near to Mr. Wright to give him the watch. The matter was reported to the police, who made dili- gent inquiries as soon as the pawnshops were opened next moning, and warned all places where prisoner was likely to try to dispose of the watch. The prisoner must have got to know of that, and just after a police officer had left Mr. Wright's house on Tuesday morning

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

It was a purely amateur eleven which did duty for Warringtm in the encounter with Newton-le-Willows at Arpley on Saturday, an attack of rheumatism pre- venting Lynes, the popular and useful professional, from appearing. The team, however, displayed pretty good form, for although they had not the satisfaction of administering defeat to their opponents, they suc- ceeded in making a draw of the encounter. The New- ton batsmen wielded the willow well and compiled 122, and to this Warrington had replied with 104 for the loss of 9 wickets when stumps were drawn. It was gratifying to note that the increased interest which is being evinced in the doings of the Warring- ton eleven was reflected by the large attendance of spectators.
R. Carson was the visitor's most useful batsman, 20 being the out Come of his innings. W. V. Turton, was responsible for 19, J. Richardson for 18, and J. Olive for 16.
Warrington had a very capable representative in T. Houghton who knocked up 45 in faultless style. P. B. Hawtin was also in good form and augmented the total by 27., W. H. Podmore compiled 12.

The second eleven tried conclusions with the Newton second contingent and had decidedly the best of matters.. Having knocked up 211 for the loss of 9 wickets the Warringtonians declared their innings and succeeded in dismissing the home team for the .aggregate of 112. Thewlis, the old Warrington pro- fessional,, batted in grand style and was responsible for no fewer than 70 runs. E. E. Woods was also to the fore with a contribution of 43, and other note- worthy totals were A. Duckworth's 33 (not out) and H. Pierpoint's 21. C. Hindley (38), and. F. Harrison (25) and A. Pendry (20), were Newton's most use- ful batsmen but most of the players failed to make headway against the deliveries of D. Plinston and W. Bennett. The Warrington fielding was also very creditable,Bennett capturing four wickets for four runs.

By the margin of a single run Sankey Wire Mills placed a victory to their credit on Saturday when lace were the opposing eleven. None of the batsmen on either side attained double figures. Burton bowled in fine style for the Wire Mills, taking 8 wickets for 14 runs.

Penketh entertained Moore and Daresbury and the encounter proved very exciting, the home team being victorious by two runs. S. Hobson (11) has the dis- tinction of being the only player to attain double figures.

An eleven representing the Warrington employes of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son journeyed to Burton- on-Trent on Saturday, and returned victors by the respectable margin of 35. W. Ashton batted splen- didly for the visitors, and ran up a total of 28. T. Wright howled effectively, capturing 5 wickets for 7 tuns.

St. Paul's sustained defeat t the hands of the Stratton and Appleton eleven, 47 and 38 being the respective totals. A.. Jones (16) was the top scorer and Norbury bawled well for the home team taking six wickets for nine runs. ,

St. Paul's 2nd fared better than the Ist contingent defeating Christ Church by a margin of 3. W. Bell (27) and S. Griffiths (13) batted in good form for the winners, W. Southern (11) obtaining the highest score for Christ Chuich.

Latchford Baptists made short work of the Bewsey- road Wesleyans as the respective aggregates-96 and 12—show. Fletcher knocked up a capital 25 (not out) for Latchford and IL Shorter contributed 12. Cliffe captuled 5 wickets for 5 runs and Wilkinson 4 for 5. ,
bheshire Lines Engineers' had little difficulty in accounting for Crosfield's eleven by a majority of 17 runs. There were no double figures on either side.

Fairfield very easily. defeated Walkers 2nd on Saturday the respective scores being 92 against 26. The batting, bowling and especially the fielding of Fairfield showed great improvement. To-day they visit an, XI. of the St. Helens Cable Co As there is friendly rivalry between these teams a very interest- ing game is expected.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

At the Halifax Cricket and Football Club sports on Saturday C. Berry of Warrington won the one lap and the one mile cycle races. On Monday at the Sheffield Charity Tournament A. E. Howard (Warrington) secured first place in the half-mile and third in the mile.

Saturday's run in connection with the Lovely-lane Cycling Club was to Hatchmere on the borders of Delamer° Forest, the journey being made via Acton Bridge, Crowton, and Norley. A good muster of members availed themselves of the opportunity of visiting one of the most picturesque spots in Cheshire and had every cause to be satisfied with the outing. The weather was all that could be desired and a most enjoyable afternoon was spent. *After tea the mem- bers strolled through the beautiful woods and before starting for home several photographs were taken and on the return journey one enthusiast obtained the Vicar's permission to photograph the beautiful little church at Norley. Warringtou was reached about 945 after one of the most successful runs of the season.

div.head: Running.
div.p: Running.

L. Green, of Warrington, won the 220 yards race at the Sheffield Charity Tournament on Monday. St. Helens runners have been going strongly of late. On Monday at Wigan Infirmary sports F. W. Webber secured third place in the mile, W. Didsbury first in the 220 yards, A. Shaw second in the quarter mile with E. Hilton Earlestown) third. A. Peachey, of St. Helens obtained a third in the 220 and second in the 100 yards at Oldham Police sports on Tuesday.

Angling. At the last meeting of the Warrington Anglers' Association, forty-three new members were proposed. The General Secretary announced that anglers' rail- way travelling facilities had been granted to the Broadheath and District A.S. through the Provincial Angling Association. Several details appertaining to the first match of the season, in connection with the Association, and which will be decided at "London Bridge," on Saturday, July 11th, were arranged. The members of the Latchford A.S. I)ave now only three vacancies on their membership roll. At their last meeting, tho date of one of their matches was altered from September tith to September 19th. The members are having an outing to Stretton to-day. The Mersey A.S. will fish their opening club match on June 21st at Vale Royal. The Perseverance A.S. will decide their opening contest at 'Vale Royal on July 6tit.

The Examiner Friday, June, 12, 1903. RUNCORN NOTES. ITHE MAYOR'S "AT HOME." [BY A CORRESPONDENT]. The rebuilding of St. Paul's roof is proceeding very rapidly indeed. The recent spell of tine weather has enabled the workmen to get the work so well in hand that it is anticipated that the edifice will be opened long before it was expected. Some time in December, it was stated, would, see the work completed, but it is now asserted that the work will be finished by Septem- ber. Unluckily the anniversary services will not be held in St. Pauls, and it is feared in many quarters that this will have a prejudicel effect on the collections. The rebuilding of the roof will cost some £2,000, and it is to be met by subscription. With reference to the accident at the Transporter Bridge when the jib of the crane broke, it is stated that the Transporter Company is trying to make the builder of the crane responsible for the breakage. The crane, it appears, is guaranteed to lift so many tons,and current talk has it that it was not lifting, by many, pounds, the guaranteed weight. LICENSING PROSECUTIONS AT RUNCORN. At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr. F 4.1. Norman (in the chair) and Mr. J. Pritchard, Thomas Bourne, licensee of the Swan Inn,Shaw-street, was summoned by Superintendent Ennion for keeping his hottse open after hours. Mr. Giles, of Chester, prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. F. A. Lake appeared for the defendant.—The evidence showed that on Sunday, 24th May, at 11.15 a.m., Superintendent Ennion, in company with P.C. Wilding, visited the house. The front way was apparently locked upzblit on going to the back door, which was open, the superintendent found the licensee seated at a small table with two men named Green and Willis, drinking beer. On being questioned defendant stated that Green was a relation who worked at Warrington while Willis was a friend who had called to look at some vegetables groin in the garden. The beer had been given to the men and no money had passed between them.—The case was dismissed.— At the same Sessions Herbert Andrews, licensee of the Elephant and Castle was charged with permitting drunkenness. Mr. Giles, Chester, again prosecuted, and Mr. Knowles, Widnes defended. The prosecution alleged that a man named Rutter, entered the house and was served while in a drunken condition with two bottles of stout. He was then ejected for drunkenness. The defence contended that Rutter was not drunk, and that he had been ejected because he had used obscene language. After a lengthy hearing the bench dismissed the case.

Harriet Taylor, Pilkington's-yard, was charged with stealing two pairs of mole skin trousers, a man's shirt, and a nightdress, the property of Teresa Corolla, wife of John Corolla, an Italian. It appeared that during the progress of the fire the prosecutor's goods were removed to prisoner's house and prisoner appropriated the articles mentioned. As this was prisoner's first appearance she was fined 20s. with the option of 14 days' imprisonment. WARRINGTON BRIGADE CALLED TO ANOTHER FIRE. The Warrington Brigade were on the point of leaving the tannery shortly after noon on Tuesday when they received information that a small farm hording, consist- ing of a thatched cottage and out-buildings in Cow. lane, Sankey, was onfire. They immediately proceeded to the scene of the outbreak and were followed by Messrs. Crosfield's Brigade, who had also been slim- moned. On arrival it was found that the fire had gained a complete mastery. The buildings were one mass of flames, and despite the strenuous- efforts of the firemen, were quickly gutted. The house was occupied by Mr. Isaac Mills, an ironworker, and Mrs. Mills who was con- fined to her bed, was only rescued with difficulty. For- tunately the furnitureland household effects were saved. The fire is supposed to have been caused by a spark from a passing traction engine igniting the, thatched roof. The property belonged to Lord Lilford,and the damage amounts to between £lsoand £2OO.
